A war secretary's letter at that hour carried the counsel of the man who had overseen the bomb from its birth. Stimson's advice joined the military and moral weight of the choices ahead. This message is part of the last counsel the president received at Potsdam. It shows the cabinet's elder hand still on the brief at the close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1413:
Secretary Byrnes answered Ambassador Caffery in Paris on 15 August 1945. The reply came nine days after Caffery's great cluster of cables to the secretary. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Replies from the secretary close the loop that cables open. After reading Caffery's six messages of 6 August, readers reach Byrnes's answer with a sense of what Washington decided to give, refuse, or postpone. The date matters too: 15 August was the day the war against Japan ended. So the reply belongs to the first day of the postwar world. The French file, like everything else, turned a page that day.
frus-1945-50-intel-d13:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent a joint memorandum to Secretary of War Henry Stimson and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal on 19 September 1945. It carried the settled view of the nation's top military body. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

When the Joint Chiefs spoke together, the armed services presented one front to the civilians above them. Their memorandum on the eve of the OSS order shows the military claiming its share in whatever intelligence system came next. Readers should weigh the channel: the chiefs wrote to both service secretaries at once, binding Army and Navy to a common line. Much of the volume's later bargaining grows from positions fixed in papers like this.
frus-1945-50-intel-d113:
Hoyt Vandenberg, the new director of central intelligence, wrote to Hoover on 3 July 1946. Vandenberg had taken over the CIG in June, full of plans to make it a real agency. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Vandenberg's arrival changed the group's pace: he wanted the SSU's operations, a bigger budget, and a clear field abroad. His first letters to Hoover opened the sharpest phase of the border war with the FBI. Readers should watch the difference in tone from Souers's careful papers. Where Souers conciliated, Vandenberg pressed. The volume's second half runs on the friction his pressing created, with departments, with the bureau, and with the White House itself.
frus-1945-50-intel-d213:
A memorandum dated 9 May 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division, Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter). It is document 213 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d313:
A letter from Secretary of Defense Johnson reached Secretary of State Acheson on 7 October 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 313 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Two years into the CIA's life, the question in these papers is less how to build it than how to fix it.

Between offices that did not answer to each other, a letter was the polite but firm way to press a point. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d413:
John Steelman, acting chairman of the National Security Resources Board, wrote to Sidney Souers of the National Security Council on 2 February 1950. The memo is document 413 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Resources Board planned how the nation's farms, plants, and workers would serve in a war. Its place in an intelligence volume shows how wide the word security had grown by 1950. Steelman's memo links war planning at home with the secret work of watching threats abroad. The Board's link to the Council gave its chairman a direct line into war planning at the top.
frus-1861-d13:
Norman Judd, the American minister to Prussia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 July 1861. The dispatch is document 13 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Judd was a friend of Lincoln's from Illinois politics, sent to Berlin that spring. Prussia was rising as the strong power of north Germany, and its stance mattered. Judd's reports told Washington how the Berlin court read the American war in its first summer. Berlin watched the war through the lens of its own struggle with Austria and France. Berlin's cool tone suited the Union, which asked no more than strict fairness.
frus-1861-d113:
Mr. Jones wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 July 1861. The dispatch is document 113 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Jones wrote on the eve of Bull Run, the war's first great battle. His July report is the second of his two papers in this file. Read with his April note, it brackets the season in which the short war became a long one. His two reports, spring and summer, frame the war's first season from one post. One post, two seasons: the frame shows how much the war had changed by July.
frus-1861-d213:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Marsh on 21 June 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 213 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d13:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 February 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 13 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d113:
Writing home was Charles Francis Adams's duty, and his letter of 31 July 1862 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 113 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d213:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 5 April 1862, in a note printed as Document 213 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, received it at the legation.

Early April 1862 brought the great battle of Shiloh in Tennessee and the start of the campaign against Richmond. Each swing of the war changed the odds that Europe might step in, so envoys traded paper at a fast rate. A note from this week sits in the file as part of that quick, watchful exchange. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d313:
On 20 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton another dispatch, printed as Document 313 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark the post-battle rush.

Seward wrote on the eve of Lincoln's emancipation announcement, which he had helped shape and knew was coming. The proclamation would give the war a cause that European publics could cheer. His letters to Paris in these days prepared his envoy for the new ground, on which defending the Union also meant defending freedom. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d413:
From Madrid on 9 November 1861, Carl Schurz sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 413 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message.

Schurz wrote in the weeks when Britain, France, and Spain had just agreed to act together in Mexico, a move that worried Washington deeply. As minister in Madrid he could watch Spanish motives at close range. His reports home fed the Union's effort to keep the European powers separate and neutral. The dispatch is part of the first season of that long campaign, before Schurz left Spain for army service.
frus-1862-d513:
Two days after Pike's latest report was dated, on 8 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 513 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The crossed dates are the Atlantic mail at work: each man wrote from news the other had not seen. Seward's August orders to The Hague kept up the standing themes of Dutch neutrality and colonial ports. They also kept up the Union's refusal to treat the rebellion as a nation. Pike's replies, arriving a month later, show how those themes landed. The pair of files, order and report interleaved, is the true shape of the record the volume preserves. It is a slow conversation. Two governments carried it on in good faith across an ocean.
frus-1862-d613:
The Danish file opens on 22 January 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen. It is Document 613 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Denmark was a small maritime kingdom. Its ports and its Sound dues touched Baltic trade. Wood, a New York lawyer, held the post through the war. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Copenhagen court. The Baltic was far from the fighting, but its states' goodwill counted in the general European balance the Department tracked. The letter begins a quiet, regular file in the volume's northern tier.
frus-1862-d713:
Luis Molina wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 September 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington, a lawyer who had long handled his land's affairs in the United States. The letter is document 713 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Foreign envoys in Washington wrote to Seward on the business between their lands and the United States. For Costa Rica, trade and the transit routes of Central America were never far from the talks. Molina's letter is part of that formal exchange, in which small republics dealt with a great power then fighting for its life. The file that follows shows the talk run both ways.
frus-1863p1-d13:
On 13 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 13 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote on the day of the battle of Fredericksburg, though its news had not yet reached London.

Letters crossed the Atlantic in about ten days by steamer, so each side wrote in the dark about the other's last moves. Seward's mail set the claims Adams was to press on Britain. They were fair dealing, a tight rein on warships built for the South, and no aid to the rebellion. This letter is one link in that chain of orders.
frus-1863p1-d113:
On 11 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of three letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 113 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three letters in a day, a week after a batch of twelve, show a desk that never let the London file cool. Seward split his points across the sheets so Adams could use each on its own. This one opens the day's set. It is part of the spring press on Britain, kept up sheet by sheet from Washington.
frus-1863p1-d213:
The mail from London dated 11 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 213 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d313:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 3 November 1862. The note is document 313 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d413: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 March 1863. It is document 413 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d513:
A dispatch dated 14 May 1863 went from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d613:
Document 613, dated 14 August 1863, records a letter from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
plos-pone-0000113:
Avihay Apatoff, Eddo Kim, and Yossef Kliger published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It tackles a practical problem in bioinformatics. The question is how to judge whether computer tools that detect homology, shared ancestry between proteins, do a good job.

Most checks of these tools lean on sequence alignment, which can bias the score. The authors work toward a scoring approach that does not depend on alignment, so different detection methods can be compared on fair terms. A cleaner yardstick helps researchers pick tools they can trust when hunting for distant protein relatives.
plos-pone-0000213:
Joana M. Ramis, Clara Collart, and James C. Smith published this developmental biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the frog Xenopus, signals called Xnrs and activin guide early development. The authors show the two signals regulate distinct sets of genes, and that activin in particular controls cell division during development.

An embryo must grow and pattern itself at the same time, and these signals help divide that labor. Separating which genes each signal controls clarifies how a ball of cells becomes an organized body. The frog work informs developmental biology broadly, since the same signal families pattern human embryos.
plos-pone-0000313:
Benoit Foligne, Georgia Zoumpopoulou, Joelle Dewulf, and colleagues published this probiotics study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Probiotics are live microbes eaten for health benefits, and how they work has been unclear. The authors report a key role for dendritic cells, the immune system's scouts, in how probiotics produce their effects.

Dendritic cells sample the gut and teach the rest of the immune system what to tolerate. If probiotics act through them, that explains benefits that reach beyond the gut itself. The paper gives the probiotic field a concrete mechanism to test, in place of vague claims about good bacteria.
plos-pone-0000413:
Sara Calhim, Simone Immler, and Tim R. Birkhead connected sperm shape to mating competition in birds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. After mating, sperm from rival males can compete inside the female, a pressure called postcopulatory sexual selection. The team asked whether species facing stronger competition have more uniform sperm.

Their title states the pattern they found: strong postcopulatory selection goes with reduced variation in sperm morphology. Uniform sperm suggests selection is fine-tuning the design tightly where competition is fierce. Bird sperm vary hugely across species, so this link helps explain what drives that variety, a long-standing puzzle in evolutionary biology.
plos-pone-0000513:
Marcelo M.S. Lima and colleagues examined a small brain region's command over sleep in rats, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The region is the substantia nigra pars compacta, better known for its role in movement and its loss in Parkinson's disease. The team studied its role in regulating sleep patterns.

Parkinson's patients famously suffer disturbed sleep, and the link is usually blamed on other brain systems. If this movement center also regulates sleep, the two symptom families share one source. Rat studies let researchers manipulate the region directly and watch sleep architecture change, something impossible to do as cleanly in patients.
plos-pone-0000613:
Themba Mzilahowa, Philip J. McCall and Ian M. Hastings examined the genetics of Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes the most dangerous form of malaria. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study tackles a live dispute about how the parasite's populations are structured. The title gives their answer plainly: the organism is essentially sexual in its reproduction.

How fast malaria can adapt matters for every drug and vaccine aimed at it. If parasite genes mix freely through sexual reproduction, new traits can spread in ways that control programs must plan for. The authors set out their evidence for that mixing. Malaria workers and population geneticists alike will find the argument worth weighing.
plos-pone-0000713:
Patrick Hossler, Bhanu Chandra Mulukutla and Wei-Shou Hu analyzed how mammalian cells process sugar chains on proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. N-glycosylation, the attachment of those chains, is key to the quality of many therapeutic glycoprotein drugs. A relatively small set of enzymes gives rise to a large number of N-glycans through a network of reactions and intermediates.

A systems analysis treats that network whole, rather than enzyme by enzyme. For drug makers, the exact sugar pattern on a protein can decide whether a medicine works and how long it lasts. Modeling the network points to which steps to tune in the cells that manufacture biologics.
plos-pone-0000813:
Kenji Matsuura, Takashi Tamura, Norimasa Kobayashi and colleagues unmasked the chemical signal termites use to recognize their eggs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Social insects rely heavily on pheromone communication to maintain their social life. Egg protection is among the most fundamental social behaviors in social insects. A fungus that mimics termite eggs, nicknamed the termite-ball, had recently been discovered, opening the study of egg recognition.

Their title names the pheromone: lysozyme, a protein better known for killing bacteria. Workers apparently read lysozyme on eggs as a do-not-eat, protect-this signal. A defensive enzyme doubling as a social label is an elegant economy, and a caution for pest control by mimicry.
plos-pone-0000913:
Diana Abdueva, Michele Wing, Betty Schaub and colleagues put two Affymetrix gene chips head to head, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene chips let labs read the activity of thousands of genes at once. The newer exon arrays promised whole genome readings at the level of single exons, the segments that get stitched into messages.

That design dropped some older features and used a new way to prepare samples. The team ran an experimental comparison against the widely used U133Plus2 array. Head to head tests like this help labs decide whether a new platform earns its claims. They also protect later studies from building on a weaker tool.
plos-pone-0001013:
Tim Schulz, Markus Glaubitz, Doreen Kuhlow and colleagues warned that a common mouse engineering tool can switch off without warning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Cre and loxP system lets researchers delete a gene in one tissue only, a standard route to knockout mice. Studies often check a tail sample to confirm the system is present.

The team report losing Cre expression in a transgenic line, which makes tail checks unreliable. A mouse can carry the gene yet not express it where it counts. Their report is a practical warning: verify the tool itself, not just its paperwork. Many published results rest on this system.
plos-pone-0001113:
Alisha Holloway and David Begun found fast adaptation concentrated in parts of proteins whose jobs are unknown, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Adaptive protein evolution is pervasive in Drosophila fruit flies. Genomic studies had usually analyzed each protein as one unit, averaging change across its whole length.

The authors argue the targets of adaptation may sit in particular parts: domains, or regions tied to folding. In Drosophila simulans they report rampant adaptive evolution in regions of unknown function. Unknown does not mean unimportant; it may mean the most interesting biology is unmapped. Their result redirects attention to the blank stretches of familiar proteins.
plos-pone-0001213:
A protein called HCF-1 helps control cell division and partners with enzymes that add or remove chemical marks on histones. Soyoung Lee and colleagues studied one histone mark under HCF-1's influence, phosphorylation of histone H3 at serine 10, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They worked in both the worm C. elegans and mammalian cells.

The authors report that HCF-1 proteins regulate the status of this mark, which is tied to chromosome behavior during division. HCF-1 was first found through herpes simplex virus, where it helps switch the virus on. Its epigenetic role in normal cells is the subject here.
plos-pone-0001313:
Nitrosylcobalamin is a drug built on vitamin B12 that delivers nitric oxide preferentially to tumor cells, which display extra B12 receptors. Joseph Bauer and colleagues tested it alongside standard chemotherapy agents, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The compound induces apoptosis through one pathway and inhibits survival signaling in cancer cells.

The authors report that nitrosylcobalamin potentiates the anti-neoplastic effects of chemotherapeutic agents via suppression of survival signaling. Two attacks are better than one if they do not simply add toxicity. Their study explores whether the B12-based pro-drug makes established drugs work harder against tumors.
plos-pone-0001413:
Maria Allhorn and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how a strep germ blunts human antibodies. The germ makes an enzyme that cuts the sugar chain on human IgG, a key class of antibody. Cut antibodies bind less well to receptors on white blood cells. That weakens the push to eat and kill germs.

The authors show how this sugar cut changes the bond between antibodies and their receptors. The change is enough to damp the immune attack. Learning this trick helps explain how strep germs slip past defense. It may also guide drugs that block the enzyme and restore antibody power.
plos-pone-0001513:
Anastasia Gardiner and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a scent gene locus in fruit flies. Gene families most often grow by copying a gene, then giving the copy a new job. A less used route is to splice one gene in new ways. The team traced that route at a scent gene called Gr39a across fly species.

They chart gains, losses, and splits of the gene's parts over time. The locus grew more complex without simple copying. Such cases broaden the tale of how scent sense evolves. Scent genes shape mating and food choice, so their change can split species apart.
plos-pone-0001613:
Marta Vicente-Crespo and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a fly protein tied to myotonic dystrophy. Proteins of this family run a switch in which gene parts are used as flies grow. That switch fails in the human ill, in part because the proteins are trapped by toxic RNA. The team studied the fly form of the protein.

They show the fly protein steers the splicing of a muscle protein and also shapes cell death. Those twin roles mirror the human protein's reach. A fly model with shared roles lets labs screen drugs fast. Hits there can then be sifted for the human disease.
plos-pone-0001713:
Pernilla Lång, Vanessa van Harmelen, Mikael Rydén, and their co-authors studied an enzyme linked to obesity in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Obesity draws macrophages, immune cells, into fat tissue, which may link fat inflammation to insulin resistance. The enzyme is TRAP, short for tartrate resistant acid phosphatase, made by macrophages and related cells.

The team reports that the monomeric, single-unit form of TRAP induces an obesity that stays insulin sensitive. That is an unusual pairing, since obesity usually brings insulin resistance with it. The full text gives the mouse or cell experiments and the metabolic measures. A form of obesity without insulin resistance is a valuable clue to which parts of fat tissue actually cause diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0001813:
Jonna Soerensen, Cemile Jakupoglu, Heike Beck, and their co-authors studied antioxidant enzymes in brain development in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The thioredoxin system is an essential regulator of cellular redox balance, the equilibrium between oxidants and antioxidants. Oxidative stress has been linked to neurodegenerative disease.

The team studied thioredoxin reductases in the brain using mice whose nervous systems lack the cytosolic form of the enzyme. The full text gives the brain development outcomes and the cell data. If the developing brain cannot manage without this redox control, the system becomes a factor in both birth defects and later degeneration.
plos-pone-0001913:
Steven Woolley, David Posada, and Keith Crandall pitted family-tree methods against each other in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When genes swap parts between lineages, a simple branching tree fails, and a network fits the past better. Many network methods exist, from statistical parsimony to median-joining, yet which one works best was unclear.

The team ran computer simulations with known histories, then scored how well each method rebuilt them. A fair race on fake data with known truth shows which tools to trust on real data. That matters for tracing viruses and other fast-changing germs, where swapped genes are common and the wrong tree misleads.
plos-pone-0002013:
Bram van Raam and co-authors asked what powers the voltage across a key membrane in neutrophils, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Neutrophils, the most common white blood cells, burn sugar for energy rather than using their mitochondria, the cell power units. Yet their mitochondria still hold a membrane potential, a voltage usually made by the respiratory chain.

The team traced the source of that voltage and compared it with other blood cells. As the title states, complex III of the chain maintains it, without the supercomplex grouping seen elsewhere. Odd wiring here reflects the neutrophil's odd, short-lived way of life.
plos-pone-0002113:
Yawei Cheng and co-authors compared men's and women's brain rhythms while watching others, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Females are usually thought to be superior in interpersonal sensitivity, the knack of reading other people. The human mirror-neuron system, which fires both when we act and when we watch others act, is considered the basic mechanism for social cognition.

Whether that system differs by gender was not known. The team measured the mu rhythm, a brain wave tied to the mirror system, in men and women. As the title frames it, they report gender differences in that rhythm. Brain data add weight to a debate long held in psychology.
plos-pone-0002213:
Wolfgang Wagner, Patrick Horn, Mirco Castoldi, and co-authors followed stem cells as they aged in the dish, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mesenchymal stem cells, which can form bone, fat, and cartilage, are a hopeful tool for cell therapy. Clinics must grow them in culture first, yet what long growth does to the cells was not precisely defined.

The team tracked the cells through long-term culture. They found that replicative senescence follows a continuous and organized course. That term means the aging of cells as they divide. Changes arrive in a set order rather than at random. Knowing that timetable helps labs judge when cultured cells are still fit for treatment.
plos-pone-0002313:
Fernando de M. Dossin, Alexandre Dufour, Elodie Dusch, and co-authors built an automated way to watch chromosome ends in a parasite's nucleus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In parasites such as Leishmania major, virulence genes often sit near telomeres, the ends of chromosomes. Telomeres cluster together in the nucleus, and their layout may help control those genes.

The team analyzed microscope images of telomeric clusters automatically, tracking how their organization changes through the parasite's life cycle. An automated count replaces slow manual scoring and makes comparisons fair. Changes in nuclear layout across life stages may track the parasite's shifts between insect and human hosts.
plos-pone-0002413:
Albanese and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Alberto Albanese, Daniele Arosio, Mariaelena Terreni, among others. Its subject is hIV-1 Pre-Integration Complexes Selectively Target Decondensed Chromatin in the Nuclear Periphery. Integration of the double-stranded DNA copy of the HIV-1 genome into host chromosomal DNA is a requirement for efficient viral replication.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002513:
Zwick and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Michael E. Zwick, Maureen P. Kiley, Andrew C. Stewart, among others. Its subject is genotyping of Bacillus cereus Strains by Microarray-Based Resequencing. The ability to distinguish microbial pathogens from closely related but nonpathogenic strains is key to understanding the population biology of these organisms.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002613:
Second, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Gérard Second, Germinal Rouhan, among others. Its subject is human-Mediated Emergence as a Weed and Invasive Radiation in the Wild. The rest of the title points to the CD Genome Allotetraploid Rice Species ( Oryza , Poaceae) in the Neotropics. The rice genus Oryza serves as a model in plant genomic studies.

One open dispute is whether its spread came from natural dispersal across oceans or from recent human action. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002713:
In 2008, Wai-Tsing Chan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was murine leukemia virus spreading in mice impaired in the biogenesis of secretory lysosomes and ca 2+ -Regulated exocytosis. The catalog record names Wai-Tsing Chan first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Retroviruses have been observed to bud intracellularly into multivesicular bodies (MVB), in addition to the plasma membrane. A further point appears in the abstract. Release from MVB is thought to occur by Ca 2+ -regulated fusion with the plasma membrane. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002813:
In 2008, Kerstin Diekmann and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was an optimized chloroplast DNA extraction protocol for grasses (Poaceae) proves suitable for whole plastid genome sequencing and SNP detection. Authorship is credited in the record to Kerstin Diekmann and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Obtaining chloroplast genome sequences is important to increase the knowledge about the fundamental biology of plastids. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002913:
Otilia Vieira, Diego Hartmann, Carla Cardoso and colleagues ran a systematic lab study of surfactants in 2008. Cheap, easy protection against both pregnancy and sexually spread disease is urgently needed. Surfactants, soap-like compounds, had drawn interest as possible microbicides and contraceptives for that dual role.

The PLOS ONE work tests surfactants in vitro, meaning in lab dishes rather than in people. It weighs their power to kill microbes and sperm against the standards such products must meet. Public health readers get a sober lab check on a much-hyped idea, before any claims about real-world use.
plos-pone-0003013:
Mika Kivimäki, Debbie Lawlor, George Davey Smith and co-authors asked in 2008 whether high C-reactive protein raises atherosclerosis. CRP marks body-wide inflammation and is linked to coronary events and early artery disease measures. Proof of a causal role would need links that survive adjustment for confounders.

Data came from the Whitehall II study of British civil servants. The paper weighs CRP concentration against atherosclerosis, the artery thickening behind heart attacks and strokes. Published in PLOS ONE, the question in the title is the point: association alone does not prove CRP drives disease. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003113:
Elisabetta Vannoni and Alan McElligott recorded fallow deer groans in 2008 to test honest advertisement. Models predict sexually selected calls should signal male quality. In most vertebrates, high quality males are larger, hold higher status, and gain higher reproductive success, so calls tied to size would be honest signals.

Low frequency groans indicate larger and more dominant males, the title reports, matching the prediction. Previous research had emphasized related links, and this study tests the call itself. Published in PLOS ONE, deer groans join a broad pattern of size written into sound. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003213:
Nataly Kacherovsky, Christine Tachibana, Emily Amos and colleagues study regulation of a yeast activator protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Post-translational modification regulates promoter binding by Adr1, a zinc-finger transcriptional activator of glucose-regulated genes. Support for this model includes activation of an Adr1-dependent gene without new Adr1 protein synthesis, and a requirement for a kinase.

The authors test whether promoter binding by Adr1 may be regulated by phosphorylation in its DNA-binding region. Readers follow a precise molecular switch in a well-studied yeast system. Details like this show how cells turn genes on fast without building new proteins.
plos-pone-0003313:
Gilles Spoden, Kirsten Freitag, Matthias Husmann and colleagues trace how papillomavirus enters cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Infectious entry of human papillomaviruses into host cells is an important step in the viral life cycle. For cell binding, these viruses use proteoglycans as initial attachment sites. Subsequent transfer to a secondary receptor molecule seems to be involved in virus uptake.

The title reports clathrin- and caveolin-independent entry of human papillomavirus type 16, involving tetraspanin-enriched microdomains. Readers learn that this cancer-linked virus uses an unusual entry route. Entry routes matter because blocking them is one way to stop infection early.
plos-pone-0007413:
Elisabeth Lippert, Thomas Karrasch, Xiaolun Sun, and colleagues studied gut inflammation in germ-free engineered mice in 2009. Limited information was available on molecular mechanisms behind Campylobacter jejuni diarrheal illness. This bacterium is a leading cause of food-borne diarrhea worldwide, yet its disease mechanisms inside the intestine remained incompletely mapped in animal models.

The authors use gnotobiotic mice lacking IL-10 and carrying an NF-kappaB reporter. These mice develop rapid and severe colitis after Campylobacter jejuni infection. Their PLOS ONE model lets researchers watch inflammatory signaling directly. The system supports studies of food-borne infection and inflammatory bowel disease.
plos-pone-0007513:
Yasuaki Takeda and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how zebrafish embryos protect their future reproductive cells. A microRNA called miR-430 silences germline genes in ordinary body cells. Only the primordial germ cells should keep those genes active. Silencing works partly by shortening the message's protective tail, which leads to its destruction. The team studied a protein, DAZL, that works against that silencing.

DAZL relieves the repression by controlling the length of the poly(A) tail on germline messages. A longer tail means the message survives and can be used. In this tug of war, DAZL safeguards the messages that future sperm and eggs depend on. The study shows tail length as a precise dial for gene control in the early embryo. Small changes at a message's end decide which cells keep their reproductive potential.
plos-pone-0007613:
Duncan Astle, Anna Nobre, and Gaia Scerif published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on attention and memory. People can attend to chosen features of what they see, like color over shape. They can also switch that focus from one feature to another. Most research tests attention on present objects. This study asked whether the same attentional set can be applied to features held in memory. Perception and remembrance were compared directly.

The results show attention reaches back into memory, not only forward into the senses. A mental filter prepared for a feature works on remembered items too. That unifies two literatures that often run apart. Everyday life demands it: we search our memories with the same questions we aim at the world. The study gives that everyday skill a controlled test. It clarifies how the mind's spotlight moves through time as well as space.
plos-pone-0007713:
Dietrich Gotzek and Kenneth Ross published a review in PLOS ONE in 2009. It takes stock of a famous model system in fire ants. A single gene, Gp-9, is tied to how fire ant colonies are organized. Some colonies accept one queen, and others accept many.

The authors sum up what Gp-9 research has shown and where it stands. The system has taught biologists a great deal about the evolution of social life in insects. It also bears on wider questions, such as how genes shape group behavior. The review marks both the progress made and the disputes still open.
plos-pone-0007813:
Sushmita Roy and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It improves computer prediction of which proteins interact with each other. Most prediction methods use protein domains as clues. Domains capture the conserved surfaces where proteins bind.

The catch is that many proteins lack domain information. Those proteins are left out of domain-based tools. The authors instead exploit amino acid composition, the recipe of building blocks in each protein. Composition alone carried useful signal about interactions. Their method widens prediction to proteins that domains cannot describe. Better interaction maps support drug and disease research.
plos-pone-0007913:
Kathleen Averette and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It traces how anthrax lethal toxin kills immune cells. Sensors inside cells, called NOD-like receptors, detect invasion and danger signals. Their activation can trigger fast cell death programs.

The anthrax toxin pries open lysosomes, the cell's waste sacs. Enzymes called cathepsins then spill into the cell body. The authors show this chain depends on one sensor, Nlrp1b. Naming the required sensor explains why some cells and mouse strains resist the toxin. It also maps a step where protection might be possible.
plos-pone-0008013:
Susana Aguilar and colleagues armed stem cells to protect scarred lungs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lung scarring, called pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens the lung until breathing fails, and no good treatment exists. The team gave bone marrow stem cells a gene for a growth factor that supports lung lining cells.

The gene could be switched on with a drug pulse, keeping control in the doctors' hands. Treated mice withstood a scarring agent that badly harms untreated lungs. Cell therapy that delivers its medicine on site and on command is a step toward real care for this grim disease.
plos-pone-0008113:
Jon Bohlin and Eystein Skjerve tested how steady a bacterium's DNA dialect stays across its genome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Each species favors certain short DNA words, a pattern called its genomic signature. Once adjusted for the genome's letter balance, that pattern can name a species from random scraps.

The team checked whether the dialect holds evenly from one end of a genome to the other. Largely, it does, which is what makes scrap-based naming work at all. The check strengthens a tool used to sort microbes in soil, water, and gut samples without growing them.
plos-pone-0008213:
Francisco Tinahones and colleagues studied fat around the adult thymus in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The adult thymus slowly turns into fat tissue with age. That fat was not thought of as a source of growth signals. Recent work by the group showed it makes factors that grow blood vessels. It also prompts endothelial cells to multiply.

The team measured VEGF gene expression in this thymus fat. They compared it with a hypoxia-related factor and with cyclooxygenase-2. Links among these signals could explain how the fat supports vessel growth. The study treats an overlooked tissue as an active player.
plos-pone-0008313:
Pushpa Malla and colleagues reported tuberculosis treatment experience from Nepal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multi-drug resistant tuberculosis cannot be cured with standard first-line drugs. Treatment is long and difficult for patients. The study described outcomes for outpatients on a standardized regimen in Nepal. Care was ambulatory, meaning patients were not kept in hospital.

Data covered patients enrolled in the national program in 2005 and 2006. The program was approved under the Green Light Committee system. Showing outpatient care can work matters for poor, rural patients. The experience offers a model for similar countries.
plos-pone-0008413:
Andrew Rhyne and colleagues warned of a fishery collapse in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Fishery management has historically been inexact and reactionary. Action often comes only after a stock is overfished or collapses. The ornamental invertebrate fishery in Florida collects animals for aquariums. Catches were increasing across a more diverse array of species.

The authors call this fishery ecologically unsound in their title's phrase, crawling to collapse. Collecting many species at rising rates spreads risk widely. Early warning may allow management before ornamental stocks crash. The study urges proactive rules for the aquarium trade.
plos-pone-0008513:
Maria Camats and co-authors study a Ras protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Ras genes are classic cancer genes that also carry normal signals. Three forms exist in mammals: H-ras, K-ras, and N-ras. Their signals shape growth in healthy and tumor cells alike. The team focus on a form called p19 H-Ras. It arises from processing of the H-ras message. They ask what it does to the cell cycle.

P19 H-Ras induces a delay between the G1 and S phases. Cells pause in a reversible quiescence state, alive but not dividing. The finding assigns a braking role to this Ras form. It contrasts with the growth push of its sister forms.
plos-pone-0008613:
Shilin Chen and co-authors validate a DNA barcode for medicinal plants in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. DNA barcoding identifies species from a short standard sequence. The plant working group recommended a two-locus barcode, rbcL plus matK. That combination discriminated many but not all plant species. Medicinal plants need reliable identification, since substitutes can be unsafe. The team test the ITS2 region as a novel barcode for those species.

ITS2 successfully identifies a high share of medicinal plant samples. Its discrimination at species level exceeds the recommended pair in their test. A better barcode helps verify herbal medicines and protect consumers. It also aids conservation of wild medicinal species.
plos-pone-0008713:
Renee Chan, Kit Yuen, Wendy Yu, and colleagues compared two flu viruses in airway cells. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used human bronchial epithelial cells grown in the lab. H5N1 bird flu kills many of the people it infects. The pandemic H1N1 virus spread widely but killed far fewer. Cell maturity might explain part of that gap.

The team grew airway cells in flat and in more mature, layered forms. They then infected each form with both viruses. Growth of the viruses and the cells' alarm responses shifted with maturity. Lab models of flu should match the real airway state closely.
plos-pone-0008813:
Joseph Poduslo, Emily Gilles, Muthu Ramakrishnan, and colleagues found where amyloid-beta grabs onto nerve cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer disease involves amyloid-beta, a sticky protein fragment. Whether plaques outside cells or buildup inside starts the damage is debated. Amyloid made inside cells must first be produced from a larger parent protein. Binding to the cell surface is an early step in that story.

A segment of amyloid, called the HH domain, provided the gripping structure. It mediated binding in rat PC12 cells and mouse brain neurons. Blocking that grip might slow amyloid's entry into cells. The address gives drug designers a precise target.
plos-pone-0008913:
Xuemin Guo, Nancy Lewis Ernst, Jason Carnes, and colleagues showed two small zinc fingers are vital for a parasite's RNA editing. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness in Africa. Most of its mitochondrial gene messages must be edited before use. Editing inserts and deletes letters to make messages readable. A machine called the editosome does that work, and KREPA3 holds it together.

Removing KREPA3's zinc finger motifs broke editing in living parasites. The same loss mattered less in test-tube assays, a telling gap. Complete editing in the real cell needs those fingers. The parasite's unique editing machinery remains a drug target.
plos-pone-0009013:
Sheng-Li Lin and co-authors traced how a hormone receptor variant can flip a cancer drug's effect, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tamoxifen usually blocks estrogen action in hormone-sensitive cancers. A newer receptor variant, ER-alpha36, lacks the usual gene-switching parts. It works instead through fast signals at the cell surface.

In endometrial cancer cells, this variant made tamoxifen act like estrogen instead. It fired two growth pathways, MAPK/ERK and PI3K/Akt, in response to the drug. A blocker becoming a trigger helps explain tamoxifen resistance. Tumours carrying the variant may need a different treatment plan.
plos-pone-0009113:
Deanna Navaroli and Haley Melikian fitted tiny glowing handles onto the brain's dopamine pump, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The dopamine transporter clears dopamine from the gaps between nerve cells. It is the main target of cocaine and of several prescription drugs. Signals inside the cell retune the pump within minutes.

The team inserted tetracysteine motifs into the pump's outer loops. Those motifs light up when a matching dye is added. Researchers can then watch the pump move and respond in living cells. Seeing the pump's response to amphetamine may clarify addiction's mechanics.
plos-pone-0009213:
Kumi Kaneko and co-authors published this insect brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It looks inside the brain of the European honeybee. Bees depend heavily on vision, and a worker's brain changes shape as she gains foraging experience. The authors focused on bee versions of three genes known from other animals.

The genes, named Futsch, Tau, and MESK2 in flies, help build and run nerve cells. Using in situ hybridization, the team mapped where each gene is switched on in the bee brain. The maps show which brain regions use these genes. That helps link bee brain structure to the visual skills that guide social behavior.
plos-pone-0009313:
Leslie Crews and co-authors published this brain disease study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lewy body diseases, including Parkinson's and dementia with Lewy bodies, share one mark: clumps of alpha-synuclein in the brain. Cells normally clear such waste through autophagy, a self-eating cleanup system. Signs pointed to that cleanup failing in these diseases.

The team compared brain tissue from patients with lab models of alpha-synuclein disease. They found selective changes in the autophagy pathway, not a blanket breakdown. Knowing exactly which cleanup steps falter matters for therapy. It suggests which parts of the system a drug should aim to restore.
plos-pone-0011413:
José Burgos and co-authors weighed in 2010 whether a health program for female sex workers on the Mexico-United States border pays for itself. Workers there face high rates of HIV and other sexually spread infections, and a counseling program promoted condom use. Funders needed to know if the infections prevented were worth the program's cost.

Their cost-effectiveness analysis compared program spending with the medical costs and illness averted when condom use rose and infections fell. Hard numbers of this kind are what health officials need when budgets force choices among many worthy programs. The border setting matters, since infections cross borders with people and one country's prevention protects both. The study gives officials an evidence base for funding, or redesigning, outreach where risk and poverty meet.
plos-pone-0011513:
Joshua Mauney and co-authors showed in 2010 how to steer stem cells toward becoming bladder lining. Tissue engineers who want lab-grown urinary tissue first need a reliable recipe for urothelial cells, the lining of the bladder and urinary tract. The team treated mouse embryonic stem cells with all-trans retinoic acid, a vitamin A relative long used to guide cell fate.

The treatment directed the stem cells to a urothelial identity through signaling involving the GATA4 and GATA6 factors. A defined chemical recipe with named internal switches is what turns stem cell promise into usable tissue. Surgeons who rebuild damaged bladders, in children born with defects and adults after cancer surgery, need exactly such lining cells. The study is an early, concrete step toward growing urinary tissue in the dish.
plos-pone-0011613:
Nicole Klein examined fossil bones of extinct sea reptiles in PLOS ONE in 2010. The reptiles, called sauropterygians, thrived in Triassic seas and are known from many fossils in Germany's ancient Muschelkalk deposits. Their family relationships have long been disputed, partly because complete diagnostic skeletons are rare.

Klein sliced long bones thin and read their inner tissue patterns under a microscope. The bone structures grouped the animals differently than expected from outer anatomy alone. Those surprise groupings challenge the accepted family tree and show how much history is stored inside fossil bone, not just on its surface.
plos-pone-0011713:
Jian-Yang Guo and co-authors studied an unhelpful partnership between a pest insect and a plant virus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Begomoviruses cause serious plant disease and depend on whiteflies to carry them between plants. The invasive whitefly Bemisia tabaci spreads many of these viruses, and how infection affects the insect's own reproduction was poorly understood.

Whiteflies feeding on virus-infected plants produced more eggs and achieved higher lifetime reproduction than those on healthy plants. The virus thus boosts its own carrier. That mutual boost helps explain the rapid joint spread of this pest and the diseases it carries.
plos-pone-0011813:
Venkata Dasari and co-authors used cord blood stem cells against brain tumour cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. XIAP is among the most important proteins that block programmed cell death, and it is raised in many cancers including human glioblastoma. It promotes invasion, spread, growth and survival of malignant cells.

The team hypothesised that stem cells from umbilical cord blood could counter glioma by driving this blocker down. Their experiments show cord blood stem cells induce glioma cell death while downregulating XIAP. The one-two effect reveals a possible natural weapon against a deadly brain cancer.
plos-pone-0011913:
Mathieu Gautier, Toby Hocking, and Jean-Louis Foulley proposed in 2010 a statistical test for finding DNA under natural selection. Cheap genotyping had begun producing huge SNP data sets for whole populations. Genome scans hunt for markers that stand out from the rest, a footprint left when selection favors one variant in a place or breed.

Their Bayesian outlier criterion judges each marker against the background pattern rather than by a fixed cutoff. A cleaner way to call outliers reduces false leads in livestock and wildlife studies alike. Since selected regions often hold genes for adaptation, the method helps researchers move from a mountain of markers to a short list worth following.
plos-pone-0012013:
Koen Peeters Grietens and co-workers investigated in 2010 why preventive malaria treatment misses pregnant teenagers in rural Burkina Faso. The treatment, given in pregnancy as SP doses, was being scaled up across sub-Saharan Africa, yet coverage with the required doses stayed far below the eighty percent goal. Adolescent pregnancies are among the least reached.

Combining several kinds of evidence, the study mapped the bottlenecks: where the chain from policy to a young woman's clinic visit breaks. Teen mothers-to-be face stigma, distance, and services designed for older women. Naming the exact breaks gives programs fixable targets instead of a general lament about low coverage.
plos-pone-0012113:
Amy Moran and H Arthur Woods studied how oxygen reaches embryos sealed inside jelly-like egg masses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sea slugs lay such masses in both temperate and polar waters, and the growing young inside can only get oxygen as it drifts in from the water around them. The shape and size of the mass can help or choke that supply.

The authors compared egg masses across regions and conditions, weighing flow, form, and the needs of the embryos. Their work shows where the limits of this simple supply line lie, and how cold polar water changes the balance. It explains why these masses take the shapes they do, and what puts embryos at risk when conditions shift.
plos-pone-0012213:
Anna Shen, Kathleen O'Leary, Richard Dubielzig, and co-authors characterized a mutant mouse with an eye disease like a human one, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mouse strain appeared by chance in their colony with an enlarged front chamber of the eye. Its cornea's inner lining had turned into layered, skin-like cells that clog the eye's drain, mirroring a human corneal dystrophy that clouds vision.

Working out the mouse's defect points to a candidate gene for the human condition. A faithful animal model lets researchers watch the disease unfold from birth and test treatments safely. It also gives families affected by this rare dystrophy a concrete lead on its cause.
plos-pone-0012313:
Jesús Gómez-Gardeñes, Gorka Zamora-López, Yamir Moreno, and co-authors modeled synchronization across the cat's cerebral cortex in PLOS ONE in 2010. Conscious perception seems to need far-flung brain assemblies flashing in step for brief moments, yet the cortex's wiring map in mammals is still incomplete. Their model organizes the cortex's functional areas into a network and asks how its sync patterns arise.

They trace a shift from local, modular synchrony toward a coordinated whole as coupling strengthens. That shift mirrors what a brain must do to bind scattered features into one perception. Network models like this guide the reading of brain recordings, where the sync itself, not just the firing, may carry the message.
plos-pone-0012413:
Karin Norrman, Yvonne Fischer, Blandine Bonnamy and colleagues compared always-on gene switches in human embryonic stem cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Researchers use promoters — DNA switches that keep genes on — to tag and track stem cells. A switch that fades or varies ruins long experiments, yet promoters were rarely compared head to head in these cells.

The team tested several common promoters side by side for strength and steadiness. Some held their output far better than others during culture and differentiation. The ranking gives stem cell labs a practical guide, helping them pick switches that keep reporter genes honest from the first dish to the final cell type.
plos-pone-0012513:
Delphine Fradin, Keely Cheslack-Postava, Christine Ladd-Acosta and colleagues searched for parent-of-origin effects in autism, in a 2010 PLOS ONE genome study. Autism is strongly heritable yet genetically tangled, and most scans ignore whether a gene copy came from mother or father. For some genes, origin matters, because only one parent's copy is switched on.

Scanning sixteen thousand DNA markers with linkage methods that track parental origin, the team found regions where origin changed the effect. Such regions would be invisible to standard scans. The results argue for origin-aware analysis in autism genetics, which may recover heritability that past studies missed.
plos-pone-0012613:
Boisson, Kiyombo, Sthreshley and co-authors ran a field trial of a home water filter in the Congo. Cleaning water at home can cut germs and may prevent diarrhoea, a major killer of young children. Yet many past trials were open to bias, because families knew who got the real filter.

Their 2010 trial used a placebo filter and random assignment to keep the test fair. Households used the new device in daily life while the team tracked health and water quality. Careful trials like this one show what home filters can truly deliver in poor rural settings.
plos-pone-0012713:
Govindaraj, Manavalan, Lee and co-authors built a computer model of a little-known human immune sensor, TLR10. Toll-like receptors spot germs by their chemical signatures and raise the alarm. TLR10 sits in a family group with TLR1, 2 and 6, yet its own target stayed unclear.

Their 2010 modelling study predicted the sensor's shape and screened for molecules it might bind. Candidate ligands give lab teams a concrete list to test. Filling in the last blanks of this receptor family sharpens the whole picture of innate immunity.  Models of this kind guide costly lab work well.
pmc-2584113:
Hulsen, de Vlieg, and Alkema present BioVenn, a web tool for comparing biological lists with Venn diagrams. Genomics projects produce many lists of genes or proteins. Seeing how lists overlap helps researchers spot shared and unique items at a glance.

BioVenn draws diagrams whose areas are proportional to list sizes, so big overlaps look big. Users can paste lists into the web page and read the picture directly. A truthful picture prevents a common error: treating a tiny overlap as large. Simple visual checks like this are a first step in most gene list work.
pmc-2852313:
Emsley, Lohkamp, Scott, and co-authors describe the features and development of Coot, a molecular graphics program. Coot helps researchers build and adjust models of proteins and other large molecules by hand, guided by experimental data. Model building is the stage where a rough atomic map becomes a finished structure.

The paper presents the program's current state and the tools it offers for fitting, checking, and refining models on screen. Coot made careful hand building faster and more reliable, and it became the everyday workbench in many crystallography labs worldwide.  Interactive graphics keep the user in control of each building decision made.
pmc-3270013:
Patel and Jain present the NGS QC Toolkit for quality control of next-generation sequencing data. New sequencing technologies generate huge amounts of sequence data at high speed. Checking that data for quality is extremely important, since errors flow into every later analysis.

The toolkit offers efficient tools to trim, filter, and report on raw reads before use. Highly efficient checking matters when datasets hold millions of reads. Routine quality control became a required first step in genomics, and toolkits like this one made it practical for ordinary labs.  Sequencing centres run such checks before releasing data to public archives anywhere.
pmc-4053813:
Wood and Salzberg introduced Kraken in 2014, a program that names the source of DNA pieces very fast. In metagenomic work, a sample holds DNA from many species at once, and each piece must be assigned to a taxon. Older programs for this task were slow and heavy on computing power.

Kraken assigns labels using exact matches against a reference database, which keeps it both fast and accurate. That speed lets labs classify millions of reads on modest hardware instead of turning to rough abundance estimates. It is used to profile gut microbes, check food and water, and spot pathogens in clinical samples.
pmc-4383913:
Forbes, Beare, Gunasekaran, and their colleagues described COSMIC in 2014. COSMIC is a catalogue of somatic mutations in human cancer, the changes that arise in body cells during life. It is billed as the world's largest resource of its kind.

Release seventy, from August 2014, recorded more than two million coding point mutations. Each entry ties a mutation to the cancer samples where it was found. Oncologists and geneticists use the catalogue to judge whether a tumor's mutation is known and what it might mean. That shared knowledge helps match cancers to treatments and guides new drug studies.
pmc-4939913:
Morrison and Preston reviewed in 2016 how gut microbes form short chain fatty acids and what those acids do. They form through a tangled interplay of diet and gut microbes inside the colon. What a person eats shapes which microbes grow and what they produce.

The discovery of receptors on many cell and tissue types, for which these acids are the natural triggers, changed the picture. Short chain fatty acids are not just waste or fuel; they signal to the body and shape metabolism. They affect gut health, energy balance, and immune function. The review links diet, microbes, and host metabolism in one frame.
pmc-5465813:
Panche, Diwan, and Chandra gave an overview of flavonoids in 2016. Flavonoids are a group of natural substances with varied phenolic structures. They occur across the plant world: in fruit and vegetables, grains, tea, wine, and the bark, roots, stems, and flowers of many plants.

These plant products have a long reputation for health benefits. Efforts are being made to isolate the individual compounds and pin down how each one acts. Flavonoids are studied for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions, among others. The overview gathers their sources, types, and reported effects in one place. It serves readers who want the science behind claims for plant-rich diets and supplements.
pmc-6420413:
Jonathan Peirce, Jeremy Gray, Sol Simpson, and coauthors presented PsychoPy in its second major form in 2019. PsychoPy builds experiments for psychology, neuroscience, and linguistics. It gives precise control over what appears on screen and when.

Users can build studies with a visual builder or write Python scripts for full control. Timing and stimulus display are handled with care, which behavioral work demands. The software is free, which spread it widely among labs and students. Many published reaction-time and perception studies now run on it. Later versions added support for online experiments, which widened its reach still further.
pmc-7612213:
Minkyung Baek and co-authors described in 2021 a computer method that predicts the three dimensional shapes of proteins with striking accuracy. Protein shape decides what a protein does, yet working out shapes by experiment is slow and costly. The team took ideas proven at a recent international prediction contest and built a neural network that handles protein information in three tracks at once, covering sequence, residue pairs, and coordinates.

Information flows back and forth between those tracks as the network refines its guess of the folded structure. The authors show the method also handles proteins that work together in complexes. Freely released methods of this kind changed daily practice in biology, letting researchers start from a reliable predicted shape instead of a blank page.
pmc-8287113:
Connor Shorten, Taghi Khoshgoftaar, and Borko Furht surveyed in 2021 how data augmentation, artificially expanding training data, can strengthen deep learning for language. Working with text is among the most striking uses of deep learning, yet models often hunger for more labeled examples than projects can supply. Augmentation answers by creating varied new examples from existing ones.

The survey gathers the main strategies, from swapping and editing words to generating fresh sentences, and groups them by the ideas behind them. The authors weigh the gains reported for tasks such as classification and translation. For practitioners facing small datasets, the survey is a practical menu of tricks that can lift a model without collecting new data.
pmc-8662613:
Carlos Cantalapiedra and colleagues released eggNOG-mapper version two in 2021, a major upgrade of a tool that labels genes with their functions. Annotating genes automatically is a basic step in nearly every genome and metagenome study, yet doing it well at large scale stays hard. The tool works from precomputed groups of related genes, called orthology groups, so each new gene inherits carefully built functional information.

The upgrade speeds and widens that process, adding domain prediction alongside functional labels and family assignments. The authors show it handling metagenomic data, where millions of genes from mixed species need labels. Reliable annotation is the bridge between raw sequence and biological meaning, and this tool is one of its main carriers.
pmc-9252913:
Joseph Khoury and a large editorial team summarized in 2022 the fifth edition of the World Health Organization classification for myeloid and related blood cancers. The classification is part of a wider effort to catalog all human cancers in one consistent, layered system. This companion article covers the cancers of myeloid cells, the family that gives rise to most blood cells, plus related histiocytic and dendritic cell tumors.

The authors explain the new edition's structure and the entities it recognizes, noting where genetic findings have redrawn boundaries between diseases. Leukemia diagnosis and treatment planning around the world key off these definitions. The update therefore shapes which tests patients receive and which trials they can join.
pmc-9825413:
Elliot Sollis and co-authors described the GWAS Catalog in 2022, a knowledgebase of genome-wide association studies run jointly by institutes in the United States and Europe. Association studies scan genomes for variants linked to traits and diseases, and their results are a basic resource for genetics. The catalog stores those results in a detailed, standardized form that computers and people can both use.

It serves hundreds of thousands of users a year from universities, health care, and industry. The article covers how studies and results are deposited, curated, and kept interoperable with other resources. A single trusted catalog prevents the field's findings from scattering across thousands of incompatible journal supplements.
plos-pone-0359513:
Gayathri Ashok and co-authors described in 2026 their work on a peptide designed to do two jobs at once against human papillomavirus linked head and neck cancer. Some cancers of the head and neck are driven by this virus, whose proteins interfere with the host cell's controls. The team set out to build a short protein chain, a peptide, that targets the interacting proteins where virus and host meet.

Their peptide is meant to act as both an antiviral and an anticancer agent, striking the viral machinery and the cancer it sustains. Work of this kind is early stage and computational and laboratory based. It reflects a broader search for precise treatments for virus driven cancers, which differ from other head and neck cancers in cause and behavior.
plos-pone-0360513:
Nicolas Tugui, Shahinur Islam, and Daniel Heath developed in 2026 high throughput tests for how salmon and their relatives respond to salt stress at the gene level. Salmonids move between fresh and salt water, and their bodies must remodel to handle each, a process called osmoregulation. When that adjustment is stressed, by farming conditions or warming rivers, gene activity reveals the strain early.

The authors built assays that read those gene responses across several species at once and assessed how well the tests perform. Hatcheries and conservation programs could use such tools to check fish welfare and readiness for sea transfer without waiting for visible harm. The work also supports comparisons of how different salmonid species cope with changing waters.
plos-pone-0359413: Huang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on surgery for a stubborn eye disease. Mooren's ulcer is a painful sore at the edge of the cornea that resists standard care. The team reviewed past cases treated with a strategy based on how severe each case was. Follow-up ran for a long term. Their series may help eye surgeons choose steps when drugs alone fail.
plos-pone-0320713: Nyukuri and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a new way to treat HIV in Nairobi, Kenya. Instead of daily pills, patients can get long-acting shots. The team explored how patients at two large hospitals feel about the shots. One patient phrase, quoted in the title, calls the injection freedom. Knowing what patients value helps clinics roll out the shots in ways people accept.
plos-pone-0359213: Wang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on chemicals floating in the air of Qingyang, China. VOCs are gases given off by fuels, paints, and industry that can harm health. The team described which ones are present and judged the risk they pose. City air data of this kind help officials decide which sources to control first.

plos-pone-0357713:
Toshio Narimatsu and four colleagues show that eyes pronounced perfectly corrected can still see poorly in dim contrast, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They studied forty-three healthy adults at a Tokyo checkup center. All scored normally on the standard eye chart and had no eye disease history. The question was whether ordinary, non pathological short sight quietly degrades low contrast vision, the kind used to read grey print or drive at dusk.

Low contrast scores worsened as short sight grew. Eyes with milder prescriptions saw the faint chart clearly better than more myopic eyes, a gap that reached firm significance, and age chipped away at the scores too. Axial length of the eye and uncorrected vision also entered the picture. A perfect standard score, the authors conclude, does not guarantee full visual ability. Myopia care should be judged on more than the bright chart.
plos-pone-0357813:
Yuting Zhang, Hantao Li, and Jiye Li published a tracking methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their problem was keeping a lock on a moving target when sensor readings are noisy and clutter hides the path. Systems from radar to sonar face that same problem when a lost track can mean a missed threat or a failed rescue.

Zhang and her colleagues extended a tracking method by feeding the target's past path back into the process, using it to limit where the target can plausibly be. That feedback steadies the track when fresh readings jump around. The gain is practical: steadier tracks mean fewer false alarms and fewer moments when operators lose the object they most need to follow.
plos-pone-0353613:
Mayank Singh, Anuj Singh, and Abhay Kumar Tiwari tackled child mortality counting in India, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Counting deaths of newborns, infants, and children under five is hard where records are patchy. The team developed an indirect estimation technique and applied it to India and its states in a population-based study.

Singh's method gives policymakers credible state-by-state numbers to act on. Child mortality varies hugely across India, so national averages hide the places needing help most. Indirect methods use data that already exist, such as survey reports of births and deaths, and correct them carefully. Better estimates steer health spending toward the states and districts where children are most at risk.
plos-pone-0340713:
Bingyang Wu and Yongxi Yi published a 2026 theory paper in PLOS ONE on how governments should write open-source rules for artificial intelligence foundation software. Platforms and small independent projects differ greatly in size and in what compliance costs them, yet rules are usually uniform. Wu and Yi built a three-player dynamic game model to test whether tiered mandates, stricter for platforms and lighter for independents, grow a healthier ecosystem.

In the model, tiered rules beat uniform ones once the players differ enough from each other, with the best settings imposing clearly stricter duties on platforms and real flexibility for independents. Ecosystem health, the authors' composite measure of scale, diversity, and balance, improved substantially, most when platform compliance costs far exceeded those of small projects. They close with boundary conditions and an adaptive framework, arguing calibrated differences best protect innovation in AI infrastructure.
plos-pone-0357313:
Tan Arda Gedik, Vania De la Garza, and Ewa Dabrowska ask whether learning to read helps adults understand that others can believe things that are false. This skill, called false-belief understanding, is usually studied in children from literate homes. The team tested native Turkish adults, some literate and some not, on a tricky belief task plus measures of nonverbal reasoning, self-control, and timed word reading.

Reading speed stood out as the strongest predictor by far, explaining about half of the gap between people. Reasoning and self-control mattered less once reading was counted. Gedik and colleagues suggest that reading itself trains skills the belief task needs, such as handling sentences about thoughts and following written stories. The finding matters for adult literacy teaching and for psychology's literate bias.
plos-pone-0355313:
Kassandra Giragosian, Marina Davila-Ross, and Derry Taylor listen for dialects in young chimpanzees at two sites, a wildlife orphanage and a national park in Africa. Human speech differs by community, and chimp calls also carry site signatures, but whether those signatures grow with age was unclear. The team measured thousands of laughs, grunts, and whimpers from infants and juveniles and tested whether a computer could tell the two homes apart.

Calls from both ages carried site signatures, with one exception: infant whimpers did not. Juvenile calls were easier to sort by site than infant calls, so the dialect signal strengthens as young chimps grow. Giragosian and colleagues argue that social life and local surroundings help shape the voice, not genes alone.
plos-pone-0357413:
Nuo Ya Li and colleagues mine a global survey of several thousand doctoral students to ask what kind of supervisor support actually tracks with a satisfying PhD. Students in more than one hundred countries rated how often they met supervisors and how good the relationship, research guidance, and career help felt. The team then modeled overall satisfaction against each support type, checking the results several ways.

Meeting frequency looked helpful at first glance, but its link faded once support quality entered the model. Relationship quality, research guidance, and career support stayed strong and steady throughout, and also tracked whether students felt the degree met their hopes. Li and colleagues advise universities to train supervisors for depth of support, not just regular meetings.
plos-pone-0357213:
