Sadikul Haque Sadi, Md Arman Hossain, and Md Nurul Ahad Tawhid add family background to brainwave analysis in a screening system for attention deficit disorder risk in children. Diagnosis today leans on behavior reports, which are subjective. Brainwave models exist, yet they ignore income and home context, which shape brain development strongly. The team's network reads brainwaves two ways, as time traces and as time-frequency pictures, then fuses both with background data.

On a public dataset built for exactly this question, the combined system beat brainwave-only rivals on every one of four thinking tasks, with the biggest gains in catching true cases. Scores held up under a strict test that holds out whole children. Sadi and colleagues argue screening tools should use context, not pretend brains grow in a vacuum.
plos-pone-0355713:
Hale Cotuk Yucel, Ali Kaya, and Merve Arslan interview trainee special education teachers in Türkiye about what artificial intelligence could mean for their future classrooms. Fourteen trainees spoke at length. All had already taken part in AI courses or projects. Their accounts were sorted into themes. The themes covered the teacher, the child and family, schooling itself, and AI's future.

Trainees saw AI as more than a tailoring tool: some pictured it reshaping the teacher's role itself. They credited it with promise for independence skills, social practice, and daily decisions for learners with special needs. At the same time they worried about isolation, privacy, dependence, and murky ethics. Yucel and colleagues call for ethics-first AI literacy in teacher training.
plos-pone-0356813:
Lee Hill and her team set out the plan for a new Canadian registry. It will track kids born with one of two bowel flaws that need team care for life. In one flaw, the bowel lacks nerve cells. In the other, the outlet forms in the wrong way. No long-term record for these kids yet exists in Canada. The registry sits at a Montreal children's hospital. It takes in patients up to age seventeen, and tracks them till they are grown.

Clinic facts come from a standard team form used at each visit. Families fill in six tested surveys. The surveys cover life quality, toilet control, family strain, and bowel care at home. Hill and her team will search the data for what drives good results. They hope to ease the move to adult care, and to let Canadian data join world studies of these rare flaws.
plos-pone-0351713:
Víctor Juan Vera-Ponce and a large team pooled the world's research on the impostor phenomenon among medical students, the nagging feeling of being a fraud despite real achievement. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered thirty-five studies, and combined twenty-six that used the standard Clance scale, covering more than nine thousand students across many countries.

Just over half the students scored in the impostor range, though carefully sampled studies produced a lower figure near a third, warning that the headline number depends on who gets asked. Rates were similar for women and men, and for early and late training. Country differences were wide, from under a third in Peru to nearly nine tenths in the United Arab Emirates. The authors press medical schools to normalize the conversation.
plos-pone-0357013:
Hong-Nhu Nguyen, Quang Sang Nguyen, and Tan N Nguyen analyzed a hybrid network where a satellite and ground stations serve many users at once. The network uses a signal-splitting scheme called rate-splitting multiple access. Their 2026 paper derives exact formulas for the system's total data rate and error rate. The formulas assume the flickering signal conditions typical of satellite links. The team then checks the math against simulations.

Rate-splitting beat the conventional non-orthogonal scheme on efficiency and interference control. The authors trace how dividing transmit power tunes the result. The split runs between the shared and private parts of each message. Such networks are candidates for bringing broadband to remote regions in the coming generation of mobile systems. These formulas help engineers design them without endless trial simulations.
plos-pone-0354513:
Beilin Dong and colleagues redesigned the height-adjustment mechanism of a machine that torture-tests mining cables by bending them, so the machine can match the different dragging heights of real coal faces. Their 2026 engineering study built a hydraulic rack-and-pinion lifting system, modeled a heavy mining cable's material behavior from strand tests, and simulated the mechanism's moving stresses and fatigue life.

Peak stresses in the gears, guide columns, and sliders stayed within safe bounds, and the team pinpointed the guide column's limiting hole as the fatigue-critical spot. A topology optimization pass then carved away unneeded material for a lighter design. Better test rigs matter because cables that fail underground, under load and constant flexing, are a lethal hazard.
plos-pone-0355113:
Doris van der Smissen and colleagues interviewed twenty-two cancer survivors. They also ran focus groups with twenty-five health workers in the Netherlands. The question was what good support after cancer treatment actually looks like. Their 2026 study spanned survivors of different ages, sexes, and times since diagnosis. The workers ranged from hospital doctors to job physicians and informal caregivers.

Both sides converged on person-centered care, cut to fit each person. It should reach beyond medicine into work and peer contact. It should help survivors steer their own recovery. The workers added hard truths. Many doctors do not know what support exists, roles blur, and referral options lack any shared map. The study names delivery, not intent, as the failing point in survivorship care.
plos-pone-0355613:
Ali Raza and four colleagues redesign a small but crucial component of neural networks in this 2026 paper: the activation function, the curve that decides how strongly each artificial neuron fires. Standard curves are fixed, which limits how well a network can adapt to varied data. Their proposal lets the function's slope, range, and curvature adjust, in three flavors: preset by hand, learned globally by the network, or learned separately by each layer.

Across handwritten digits, fashion images, skin lesion photos, and COVID-19 scans, the adaptive versions generally converged faster and classified better than fixed functions. A compact network using the layer-wise version beat two famous deep architectures on the fashion benchmark and handled imbalanced medical classes more robustly. The authors argue that letting each layer tune its own nonlinearity is a cheap upgrade for image models that must transfer across domains.
plos-pone-0356013:
Hirotaka Eguchi and colleagues asked whether the thickness of the temple muscle, visible on routine head scans, predicts immunotherapy success. Muscle loss can weaken response to immune checkpoint drugs in returning head and neck cancer. Their 2026 study measured the muscle in just over a hundred patients treated with two such drugs.

Patients with thicker temple muscles responded to treatment more often than those with thinner muscles. One year on, both freedom from progression and survival were clearly better in the thicker-muscle group. The link held after adjusting for chemotherapy use. Eguchi and colleagues propose the measurement, free on scans patients already receive, as a simple marker for sorting patients by likely outcome.
plos-pone-0329913:
Michaela Taylor-Williams and co-authors piloted a camera that reads oxygen in the tiny vessels at the fingertip nail fold. Standard nailfold imaging shows vessel shape in systemic sclerosis, a disease that deforms small blood vessels. Their 2026 feasibility study asked whether multispectral imaging could add oxygen information to the picture.

A nine-band camera imaged twenty-two people, ten with systemic sclerosis and twelve controls. The team compared oxygen-sensitive measures across nailfold regions using statistical models suited to repeated measures. The study's aim was feasibility, not diagnosis: can the device capture usable functional signals at all? Taylor-Williams and colleagues present the pilot as groundwork for imaging that could one day separate patients from healthy people by vessel function.
plos-pone-0354913:
Muse Shomre, Dawit Meskele, and Yishak Beyene assess in 2026 water and climate trends on the eastern edge of a lake basin in Ethiopia's Rift Valley. They combined records from several weather stations and a river gauge over many decades. Trend tests, drought indices at different time spans, and checks on river flow patterns gave a joined picture.

Rainfall trends were mostly flat, but hottest monthly temperatures rose at nearly all stations. Drought grew more frequent and severe in recent decades at several places. River flow shifted too, with higher low flows and weaker peaks. Short span drought indices caught repeated dry spells best, guiding local water planning.
plos-pone-0355413:
Qinxingzi Li and co-authors chart in 2026 how common bacterial and fungal infections differ by sex, age, and season at a large Chinese hospital. Six years of test records covered the species found most often, making up nearly all positive samples. Each species was checked for patterns across the three factors and by a staining group used in microbiology.

Most species showed sex differences, almost always peaking in males, and nearly all varied by age. Summer brought the peak for many species. One staining group reacted more strongly to sex and season than the other. Prevention and testing plans should build in these patterns, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0354813:
Caitlin A Hildebrand led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study of family doctors and food. Thirty-two primary care physicians described their training, daily practice, and teamwork around nutrition, a topic central to chronic disease yet thin in medical education. The study used design thinking, learning from users to frame the problem.

Doctors valued nutrition but felt unsure where their role as generalists starts and stops. They asked for clearer expectations, handier resources, and stronger links with dietitians. Hildebrand argues training reform should follow that clarified role, so advice to patients becomes practical instead of vague.
plos-pone-0344213:
Wubet Tazeb Wondie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 systematic review of deaths among low birth weight newborns in Ethiopia. Small babies face many times the death risk of normal-weight newborns, and Ethiopian studies disagreed on the scale. The reviewers pooled fifteen studies covering more than seven thousand babies.

Lack of kangaroo mother care, cold stress, extreme smallness, and being born early all predicted death. Wondie urges strict practice of skin-to-skin care, screening, and breastfeeding, plus stronger community newborn care, to cut a toll that better routines can prevent.
plos-pone-0354713:
Ali Aranizadeh, Behrooz Vahidi, and Amir Khorsandi published this 2026 study of keeping medium-voltage electrical switchgear healthy and safe in power networks. Switchgear wears under heat, strain, and electrical stress until failures black out customers. Their framework sorts readings into four groups covering power flow, moving parts, insulation, and support, then blends scaling, probability, and fuzzy expert logic into health scores and remaining life.

Tested on real data from two substations, the method outscored older techniques in both accuracy and clarity. Aranizadeh offers it to utilities fixing gear when its state demands it, not by the calendar.
plos-pone-0352813:
Yo Muraki and six colleagues examine how an upgraded cancer cell therapy rallies the patient's own immune system, in this 2026 PLOS ONE mouse study. The therapy engineers T cells with a synthetic receptor plus two helper molecules that summon and grow immune cells. Conventional versions struggle against solid tumours. Four days after treatment of mice bearing such tumours, the team profiled the host immune cells inside them.

Tumours treated with the upgraded cells filled with the host's own killer T cells and macrophages, which conventional therapy did not achieve. Those host cells switched on inflammatory and summoning genes. The engineered cells, it seems, act as recruiters as much as fighters — a mechanism that could matter for human solid-tumour trials.
plos-pone-0353213:
David Fräulin, Irina Sidorenko, and Renée Lampe propose a radiation-free way to check the tools that monitor curved spines in teenagers, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Scoliosis affects up to three percent of adolescents, but tracking it with X-rays means repeated radiation. Camera systems that read the back's surface offer an alternative, yet proving their accuracy is tricky because surface scans and X-rays are taken at different times, in different postures.

Their fix generates the test data automatically from CT scans, extracting the outer back surface and the inner spine from the very same image. Posture mismatch disappears by construction. Clean verification data of this kind could finally let surface methods graduate from sidekick to trusted diagnostic tool.
plos-pone-0354013:
Hansa Gul and seven colleagues test compounds from a soil fungus against drug-resistant staph bacteria that infect cow udders, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Resistant Staphylococcus aureus shrugs off antibiotics partly by pumping them out of the cell. The team profiled the fungus's chemistry, tested its extract against the bacteria in dishes, and used computer docking to see whether its molecules could jam four of those pumps.

The crude extract stopped the bacteria in a clear ring on the plate, and two isolated compounds matched that performance. Simulations showed several fungal molecules binding the pumps stably. Blocking the pumps rather than killing the bacterium outright is a promising flank attack on resistance, though animal testing lies ahead.
plos-pone-0338813:
Bardel and colleagues fed laying hens hormones and plant extracts to test chick sex outcomes in a 2026 study. One hundred older breeder hens were split into five diet groups for five weeks: plain feed, two hormone additions, fennel extract, and garlic extract. Blood hormones were checked twice, and late eggs were hatched.

Fennel raised a male hormone in the blood across the study. Garlic, fennel, and one hormone each raised the female share among chicks, while the other hormone shifted results the other way. Egg producers value hens over roosters, so a feed-based nudge to sex ratios would carry real economic weight if it holds at farm scale.
plos-pone-0349313:
W. Gregory Hood reports this 2026 PLOS One field study on beavers living in tidal wetlands of the Pacific Northwest coast. Beavers are usually pictured in rivers and lakes, where their dams turn flowing water into ponds. Hood surveyed tidal river deltas and estuaries in coastal British Columbia and in Washington and Oregon, where tides can rise and fall by several meters each day.

He found beaver dams throughout these tidal systems, flooded at high tide and holding water back only at low tide so the animals can move about. Tidal dams were packed more densely than river dams reported elsewhere, though somewhat smaller, and some have lasted at least thirty-five years in aerial photos. The findings argue that beavers likely shape tidal marshes, important habitat for young salmon, as strongly as they shape rivers.
plos-pone-0353113:
Duc Khanh Nguyen, Thanh Tuan Tran, and Van Sy Hoang compare two admission tools for heart failure in this 2026 PLOS One study. Both aim to predict who will die within a year. One is a blood marker of heart strain. The other is a clinical score called AHEAD, built from age and several conditions. The cohort followed four hundred thirty hospitalized patients. About one in five died during the year.

The blood marker clearly out-did the score. Each doubling of it came with roughly double the risk of death. The score predicted death on its own. But it added nothing once the marker was known. Combining the two did not beat the marker alone. The highest-marker third of patients were high risk, whatever their score said. The authors still recommend testing in other hospitals before practice changes.
plos-pone-0326013:
Jared Charlton-Webb and six colleagues set out a study protocol, published in 2026, for patients measuring their own vital signs in emergency care. Crowded departments often miss or delay basic checks like pulse and blood pressure. A smartphone tool offers a workaround. Patients record a thirty-second face video, and camera-based software estimates their vital signs. The study will run across three urgent care services in London.

Fifteen hundred patients will be measured both ways, manually and by phone. Surveys afterwards will judge whether the approach is workable and welcome. A small group of triage clinicians will rate staff acceptance. Ten thousand more patients will answer questions about digital health tools generally. As a protocol, this entry describes a plan, not results. Its findings should later show whether self-recorded vitals can safely ease triage pressure.
plos-pone-0351113:
Jafar Keighobadi and Farnaz Imani worked on calibrating an atomic gyroscope, a sensor that measures rotation by splitting atoms rather than spinning parts. Such sensors promise very precise navigation, but small biases and unknown settings spoil accuracy. Lacking a physical unit to test, they fed real flight-path data from standard navigation systems into a software model of the gyroscope.

A two-stage Kalman filter, a method that learns while it tracks, estimated the sensor's bias and settings at the same time. Bias uncertainty shrank by orders of magnitude, and orientation accuracy improved by about a third over the uncalibrated model. The approach offers a cheap rehearsal for calibration before costly hardware is built. It also explores which laser wavelengths best drive the sensor, a detail that shapes future designs.
plos-pone-0351313:
Junhao Li and Yiran Wang built a chip-based test that measures six cancer-related markers at once, all tied to how tumors invade and spread. The usual lab route tests markers one at a time, slowly, with large machines and much blood. Their platform uses a microfluidic chip, channels thinner than hair, with magnetic particles and glowing tags to catch each marker in parallel.

The six targets include enzymes and signals that help cancers break tissue barriers and grow blood vessels. The team checked the basics any test must prove: a straight measuring range, the smallest amount it can detect, repeatability, and freedom from mix-ups between markers. A single small sample yielding six invasion markers at once could speed decisions in clinics without big laboratories, and lets doctors follow several warning signs across a patient's treatment.
plos-pone-0350613:
Numbing the nerves running to the shoulder lets surgeons operate while using less general anesthetic. Hang Su and colleagues tested whether adding butorphanol, a pain drug, lets doctors use a weaker numbing solution, in this 2026 PLOS One trial with shoulder surgery patients.

Fifty patients were split between plain ropivacaine and ropivacaine mixed with butorphanol, guided by ultrasound. Each next patient's dose rose or fell depending on the previous patient's response, a staircase method that homes in on the middle effective strength. Forty patients finished. The mixed solution worked at a clearly lower strength, suggesting the added drug stretches the numbing effect and may spare side effects.
plos-pone-0351213:
Long-acting HIV treatment by injection usually means clinic visits, but trained friends or family could give the shots at home. Beth Bourdeau and colleagues built a selection tool helping patients pick the right treatment buddy, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

The team interviewed clinicians, patients, and candidate buddies to learn what makes a buddy suitable, then drafted questions and piloted them with seven patients. A community panel reviewed wording for clarity and completeness. Picking the right person, one participant said, can make or break the whole deal. The finished tool weighs trust, steadiness, and practical skills so home treatment stays safe.
plos-pone-0351413:
Jingjing Yan and colleagues set out a plan, not finished results, for comparing types of gardening therapy for older adults. The planned review covers older people whose memory and thinking have weakened and who often feel low in mood as well. Gardening care can differ in setting, soil or other growing base, and how active each person is.

Under the plan, the team will search eight large databases for trials where gardening was added to usual care. Two reviewers will screen studies, pull out the data, and judge bias with a standard tool. They will then rank the gardening types for effects on thinking skills and low mood. No findings are reported yet, because the review is still to be done.
plos-pone-0349513:
Xinghai Pu and colleagues tackle hidden faults in the buried metal grids that keep power substations safe. Old search methods miss how grid parts connect, so fault spots stay vague. Their method draws the grid as a map of nodes and links, then trains a graph based learning model on fused data from electric checks, heat images, and field sensors.

Training also bakes in physical connection rules, so answers name the exact faulty wire segment rather than a rough zone. Tests at a large substation showed clear gains in accuracy over older routes. Precise fault maps mean crews dig once, in the right place, and return a risky grid to safe service faster.
plos-pone-0350513:
Bernadette Walter and colleagues screened newly arrived asylum seekers in Heidelberg, Germany, in late summer and autumn 2024 for diphtheria and resistant wound germs. Europe had seen a rise in diphtheria among asylum seekers in the two prior years. Just over one thousand arrivals gave throat swabs, wound swabs where relevant, and survey answers, with blood tests in a subset.

No toxin making diphtheria germs were found. Among thirty seven people with inflamed wounds, about half carried resistant staph germs, near two percent of all arrivals. Over a third of those blood tested lacked protective diphtheria antibody levels. Screening found little active diphtheria, but thin immunity argues for catch up vaccination on arrival.
plos-pone-0349413:
Ajay Malhotra and colleagues used United States Medicare payment data from 2017 to 2021 for over thirty three thousand diagnostic radiologists to compare women and men. Women made up about one quarter of the group. Practice setting, subspecialty, service volume, patients served, and payments were compared in detail.

Women clustered more in academic posts, urban areas, large practices, and breast imaging, where they formed nearly two thirds. On average women received about eighty six percent of mens Medicare payments, billed fewer services, and served fewer patients. Gaps persist even in a specialty often seen as flexible, which points leaders to workload and referral patterns, not just pay scales.
plos-pone-0350813:
María Yehisiri Martín–Báez and Candelaria de la Merced Díaz-González surveyed school teachers on Gran Canaria in 2026 about pupils with type one diabetes. Teachers often give daily help to these children, and negative attitudes can put safety at risk.

Staff at seven public schools for young children answered a tested questionnaire on attitudes and bias. About half of those invited took part, fewer than the study needed for firm claims. A share said they currently teach a child with diabetes. The results give local schools a starting picture of where training and support for teachers should be aimed.
plos-pone-0342713:
Lei Zhengyao led a computer study of blood flow in a narrowed brain artery. Such narrowing is a major cause of stroke. Doctors often judge risk by how tight the narrowing looks. But blood thickness also varies from person to person. The team rebuilt a real artery scan in a model. They made mild and severe versions of the narrowing. Then they ran blood of three grades of thickness through each.

Flow turned on both factors at once. A severe narrowing made fierce stress on the wall inside the tight spot. Past the spot, flow turned slow and swirled. One stress measure even fell at the worst narrowing. The team says risk checks should add blood traits and flow measures.
plos-pone-0349013:
Miao Zhao led a survey of women students at two Chengdu universities. The topic was the virus called HPV and its vaccine. The team compared health majors with all other majors. They graded what each group knew, basic and deep. They also asked who would take the shot. Near twelve hundred forms were fit to use.

Basic facts were known in part. Deep facts were known by few. Health majors scored higher on most counts. They also showed more will to take the shot. City roots and more cash to live on tracked with will too. The math showed one clear lever: basic facts. Raise them, and will to vaccinate rose. The team backs plain, clear teaching for non-health students.
plos-pone-0350013:
Lingfeng Chen, Fengzhu Guo, and Chunlin Hong used gene data to search for what severe pancreatitis and sudden lung injury share at the molecular level. Severe pancreatitis can trigger lung damage, and the pair together are dangerous. The team combined mouse lung datasets for both conditions with blood data from human pancreatitis patients in a public database.

Ninety-four genes changed in the same direction in both mouse conditions, out of hundreds altered in each. Network analysis grouped these genes into shared pathways and highlighted hub genes that sit at busy crossroads. Checking the human data supported the same pathways across species. The short list of genes gives drug and diagnosis researchers concrete targets to test in the laboratory.
plos-pone-0349613:
Moein Yoosefi and colleagues charted how long emergency patients in Newfoundland and Labrador wait to first see a physician, and projected the trend to 2026. Records from 2015 to 2021 covered rural and urban departments and the middle urgency bands of Canada's triage scale. A statistical model separated the effects of place, urgency, and time, and simulations attached uncertainty ranges to the forecast.

The projected average wait grows from about an hour and a half in 2015 to nearly three hours in 2026, close to double. Waits are the pressure gauge of an emergency system, and a credible forecast lets a province argue for staffing and redesign before the gauge hits red. Rural departments, far from backup, are watched especially closely in the analysis.
plos-pone-0335813:
Hannah Williams and colleagues examined how gun injuries changed in central and southeastern Ohio as the COVID-19 pandemic hit, a pairing sometimes called a dual pandemic. They drew on a regional trauma registry covering twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-one, with nearly four thousand patients hurt by firearms. They modelled how injury counts, patient handling, and related problems shifted when lockdowns began and ended.

Nearly every measure jumped or changed direction at the start of the pandemic period, and shifted again when it closed, while hospital stays stayed about the same length. The authors point to rising substance use and more deliberate, non-accidental shootings as part of the surge, with signs of strain on trauma services as lockdown wore on. They call for region-specific work on what drove the rise.
plos-pone-0338613:
Liang Ge and colleagues explored whether a blood measure called the hemoglobin glycation index tracks with thinking skills in older Americans. The index compares a person's long-term sugar marker against what their recent glucose would predict, capturing how readily someone's blood proteins soak up sugar. Data came from a national health survey of more than fourteen hundred older adults who took three standard thinking tests.

Both extremes fared worse. People with the lowest and highest index values scored below those in the middle on memory and processing speed measures, even after many adjustments. The pattern differed by sex and by whether people took diabetes medicine. The authors suggest the sweet spot sits in the middle, and that this cheap index, already computed from routine blood work, might help flag older adults at risk of decline.
plos-pone-0347313:
Zhaonan Ban and colleagues fingered a cell-division protein as an accelerant of rheumatoid arthritis, the autoimmune disease that inflames and erodes joints. Mining public arthritis datasets showed the protein's gene network glowing with immune activation signals. In lab experiments, the team silenced the gene in joint-like cells and in macrophages, the immune cells whose aggressive form pours out inflammatory messengers in arthritic joints.

Silencing worked on every front: the joint cells grew and migrated less, and the macrophages failed to mature into their inflammatory form, with their surface marker and messenger output both dropping sharply. The authors conclude the protein helps drive the disease by pushing macrophages into attack mode. They nominate it as a drug target in a condition where many patients still lack a treatment that truly works for them.
plos-pone-0346413:
Malinda Desjarlais examines whom people blame or credit when feedback on their Instagram photos goes well or badly. Likes and comments can sway mood and self-worth, but the explanations users give themselves matter too. In the 2026 study, students were told a photo of theirs had been posted and then received made-up praise or criticism, after which they wrote down what they thought caused it.

Photos of the self, whether self-taken or taken by others, drew explanations pointed inward, often about looks. Meme posts instead drew explanations pointed at the audience. Students knew society judges selfie posters, yet rarely blamed that bias. The pattern shows how posting self-images can turn outside judgment into self-judgment.
plos-pone-0346713:
Xuanhuang Chen and co-workers test a light-based guidance system for placing screws into the small bones of the neck. Neck screws must be exact, since nerves and blood vessels sit close by. Their 2026 study uses cow neck bones as stand-ins, planning screw paths on scans first, then guiding real placement with structured light that maps the surface during the mock procedure.

Every one of the more than one hundred test wires landed in the safest grade of placement. Entry points missed the plan by less than a millimeter on average. The light scan lined the model up with the plan almost exactly. Such guidance could make a delicate operation steadier, though human trials remain ahead.
plos-pone-0348713:
Xiao Liang, Andrew F. Teich, and Lenwood S. Heath trace how old human genes active in the brain and immune system really are. Their 2026 study follows more than a thousand such genes across thirty-one primate species and four other mammals, comparing them with random genes and with one gene picked from each family.

Brain genes turned out older on average, reaching back before primates appeared, and they were kept by most species since. Immune genes looked younger by comparison. Genes active in both systems leaned toward the brain pattern, suggesting they served the brain first and took on immune roles later. The history hints that the brain's toolkit is deeply ancient and hard to replace.
plos-pone-0348013:
Bicky Yadav and Megha Arakeri design one combined system for sending medical scans safely over weak networks. Hospitals must shrink huge images without losing diagnostic detail, keep them secret in transit, and prove they were not tampered with. Their 2026 paper joins near-lossless squeezing, scrambled encryption, future-proof key exchange, and a shared ledger that logs only harmless proof data.

A fine-tuning layer caps how far any pixel can shift, guarding fine detail. Keys are tied to each image's own identity data rather than managed loosely. The ledger entry lets receivers verify where an image came from. Putting the steps in one design aims to close gaps that appear when each step is bolted on alone.
plos-pone-0349113:
Ivaan Pitua and co-workers set out a plan to review wasting and muscle loss among children with cancer in Africa. Malnutrition is the most common side problem in these wards and worsens survival, yet bedside checks may miss it. Their 2026 protocol describes a review of studies from the year two thousand onward across four major databases.

Two reviewers will screen studies separately and grade their quality with a standard tool. The review will pool how common wasting is, compare measuring methods such as arm tapes against weight charts, and link wasting to harms like infection and treatment dropout. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; it targets a hidden burden that better measuring could expose.
plos-pone-0348313:
Lily Soto and co-workers take a snapshot of which HIV strains circulated in the Dominican Republic in twenty twenty-four. The Caribbean carries a distinct older branch of the commonest strain, and tracking it guides care and vaccine thinking. Their 2026 study sequences parts of the virus from twenty-six patients in two cities and tests which gene regions sort the branches reliably.

Nearly every sample belonged to the usual strain, and most of those sorted to the Caribbean branch. Two gene regions sorted branches dependably, while a third did not. One sample proved to be a mixed form common in Africa and Europe, a first for the country. Even one odd strain shows why ongoing virus watching matters on the island.
plos-pone-0348413:
Anne Elizabeth Glassgow and a large team lay out the design of a five-year study of new mothers in American cities. Maternal deaths and serious complications run far higher in the United States than in other wealthy countries, and long-term stress is a suspected driver. Their 2026 paper is a protocol: it describes the study they will run, following two hundred women after childbirth.

The team will combine neighbourhood data, medical records, and interviews about trauma and support with blood tests that read chemical marks on DNA and measure inflammation and stress hormones. The plan is to trace how hard lives get written into the body. As a protocol, it reports no results yet.
plos-pone-0346813:
Lukas Waltenberger and colleagues created software that estimates the sex of people whose cremated remains survive only as burnt bone fragments. Archaeologists need this to rebuild ancient funeral customs and populations, yet cremation destroys the pelvis and skull features normally used. Their 2026 tool, called CRISP, was trained on a prehistoric Italian sample where grave goods hinted at each person's sex.

The program uses measurements from up to twenty-one surviving bones inside a Bayesian model, which reached about eighty-nine percent accuracy, beating simpler cut-off rules. A test on Austrian remains confirmed the approach travels across regions. CRISP is released openly, and can even flag deposits mixing more than one person.
plos-pone-0348113:
Metogbe Belfrid Djihouessi and colleagues review forty years of work on Benin's Porto-Novo Lagoon. Their review appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The city lagoon feeds fishers and local trade. It also suffers nutrient overload and plant blooms. Bouts of low oxygen strike it too. These ills have grown worse since the 1980s.

The review asks if Benin could report the lagoon's health under a UN clean-water goal. It also tests a European-style health grading for gaps. Basic measures are partly tracked now. Acidity, oxygen, and phosphate are among them. Other needed data are missing. The authors map what exists and what is lacking. Managers get a clear place to start.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Names, not laws, fill this Council text on the Yugoslavia court. On 26 July 2005, it adopted Resolution 1613. The court, built by Resolution 827 in 1993, used stand-in judges to widen its trial capacity. Candidates reached the Council through the Secretary-General. The Assembly then elects the judges from the Council's list.

The text sends thirty-five names to the Assembly. The nominees come from many states, from Pakistan and Nigeria to Canada. Latvia and Jamaica are on the list as well. Such staffing steps were routine work for the Council. They kept the court's rooms staffed through its busiest trial years. Each name had to pass the Assembly vote to serve.

Resolution 1413 is a UN Security Council extension of the Afghanistan security force, adopted unanimously on 23 May 2002 under Chapter VII. The International Security Assistance Force, created after the Taliban's fall to protect Kabul and the interim Afghan government, had been led by Britain, and Turkey had offered to take command.

The resolution extends the force's authorization for six months beyond 20 June 2002 and authorizes participating states to take all necessary measures to fulfill its mandate. It thanks Britain for organizing and leading the force and welcomes Turkey's offer to assume the lead. The force it kept in being later expanded nationwide under NATO.

Three months of cover for the Sahara mission came from this spare text of 2003. On 28 October, the Council adopted Resolution 1513 without dissent. It recalls the Council's past Sahara texts. One stands out: Resolution 1495 of July 2003. That text backed the envoy's peace plan as the best path for the territory.

One step does the work here. MINURSO's mandate runs to 31 January 2004. A report from the Secretary-General is due before that term ends. The bridge kept the mission in place while replies to the plan hung fire. The Polisario Front had accepted the plan by then. Morocco had not, and the gap stayed open.

Few Council demands are as short, or as blunt, as this one of 1972. On 28 February, it adopted Resolution 313 without dissent. Israel had struck into Lebanon by ground and air. The raids answered guerrilla attacks from across the border. Lebanon brought the matter before the Council.

One sentence carries the whole text. Israel must halt and shun all ground and air action against Lebanon at once. All its forces must leave Lebanese soil. The brevity is itself the message. Most Middle East texts balance calls on both sides. This one speaks to a single party, in command voice, with no softening clauses at all.

Siam, the country now called Thailand, applied to join the newborn United Nations in 1946. It had never been colonized, but the war had left its status tangled. A dispute with France over border territory had to be settled first. The Council noted that its members unanimously approved the application.

Resolution 13 then recommends Siam's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly admitted Siam in December 1946. It was among the UN's earliest new members. The country's later name change to Thailand did not affect the seat. This short text preserves the formal step by which a Southeast Asian kingdom joined the postwar order at its very start.

Negotiations over Western Sahara gained rare momentum in 2007 and 2008. Morocco offered an autonomy plan in April 2007. The Polisario Front tabled its own proposal a day earlier. Four rounds of direct talks followed. Resolution 1813, adopted on 30 April 2008, tried to keep that process alive after the Secretary-General's latest report.

MINURSO, the UN mission in the territory, was extended until 30 April 2009. Members demanded respect for the ceasefire agreements. They told both parties to negotiate in good faith, without preconditions. Realism and compromise were called essential. The text also backed family visits between separated relatives, by air and possibly by land. Money from member states was sought for such confidence-building steps.

Another year of scrutiny for Sudan's sanctions began with Resolution 1713. It was adopted on 29 September 2006. A Darfur peace deal existed, but key rebel groups had refused to sign. Violence and impunity were getting worse. Aid workers faced growing danger. The expert panel's final report had landed that August.

Members extended the panel until 29 September 2007. A fifth expert was added to strengthen it. The panel owed an interim report within ninety days. A midterm briefing was set for 29 March 2007. Non-signers were urged to join the Darfur agreement at once. Signers were told to honor it. All parties had to halt attacks on civilians.

Vietnam had been shut out of the UN for years by vetoes. The war ended in 1975 with the land made one. Saigon fell, and a single state took shape. Its bid for a seat had been blocked in 1976 by the United States. In 1977 the mood had changed. Resolution 413 passed by common consent on 20 July 1977.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam. The Assembly did so that fall. Hanoi took the seat with no foe at the gate this time. The vote closed a long tale. The UN had split the land's fate in the 1950s. War and cold rivalry kept a seat out of reach for a full age. Now the one state took its place.

Cast out by Malaysia in August 1965, Singapore stood alone. The rich port city had not sought the split. It had to build a state from scratch, fast. A bid for a UN seat came at once. Resolution 213 passed with no dissent on 20 September 1965.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Singapore. The Assembly did so the next day. Lee Kuan Yew led the new state. Few gave the small isle much hope then. It had no farms, no oil, and a port as its chief wealth. Time proved the doubters wrong. The seat was a first shield for a weak new state. This one-line text is the legal start of Singapore's life among nations.

Resolution 1313, adopted on 4 August 2000, extends the UN mission in Sierra Leone while admitting the peace there has broken down. Rebels of the Revolutionary United Front had attacked and detained UNAMSIL peacekeepers that spring, breaking the Lomé Peace Agreement. The Council praised the mission and its commander for pushing back against the threat.

The mandate was extended only until 8 September 2000. The Council judged that the rebels' widespread and serious breaches since May had destroyed the cooperative climate the agreement assumed. Until security allowed progress toward a settlement, it said, the mission's structure, strength, resources, and mandate all needed beefing up, and it signaled its intent to order that strengthening next.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 13, from the first session in 1946, organized the United Nations Secretariat. The Assembly directed the Secretary-General to build an office setup that could serve all the organs well. It listed eight main units. They included departments for Security Council affairs, economic affairs, and social affairs. They also included trusteeship, public information, legal work, and finance.

Further parts approved the public information plan kept in annex I. They adopted the provisional staff regulations kept in annex II. The text also set pay for senior posts. It backed tax relief for staff salaries. It ordered work on a job grading plan, a provident fund, and a lasting retirement scheme.

General Assembly resolution 69/13 (2014) surveys cooperation between the United Nations and the Black Sea Economic Cooperation Organization, the regional body holding observer status since 1999. The Assembly values its members' work across energy, transport, trade, environment, and crime control. It singles out joint transport projects such as the Black Sea Ring Highway. It urges international financial institutions to help fund project studies. It invites stronger dialogue between the secretariats and cooperation from United Nations agencies. A report is due at the seventy-first session.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 113, adopted unanimously on 4 April 1956, finds that tension along the armistice lines in Palestine could endanger international peace. The steps earlier resolutions required had still not been carried out. It asks the Secretary-General, as a matter of urgency, to survey how the four General Armistice Agreements are being enforced. He is to arrange measures with the parties. Those include withdrawal of forces from the lines and full freedom of movement for United Nations observers. He is to report back within one month.

In March 2010 the future of the United Nations Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad, known as MINURCAT, was still unsettled. Chad's government and the United Nations were still discussing what should happen to the mission. Resolution 1913 simply extended the mandate until 15 May 2010, on the same terms as before. The Council said the situation in the region remained a threat to international peace and security. The short extension kept the mission in place while the talks went on.

Yugoslavia was breaking apart in fighting in the autumn of 1991. The federal army faced forces in Croatia and Slovenia. Cease-fire deals signed that September were already breaking down, and the loss of life was heavy. Yugoslavia itself had welcomed a meeting of the Council. Resolution 713 was adopted on 25 September 1991.

The Council praised the peace efforts of the European Community and of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. Then, acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, it ordered a general and complete arms embargo. All states had to stop deliveries of weapons and military equipment to Yugoslavia at once. The embargo would last until the Council decided otherwise. It was meant to help establish peace and stability in the country. The Council kept the matter on its agenda until a peaceful solution was achieved.
un-sc-res-1613:
Short-term judges for the Yugoslavia war crimes court were being selected in the summer of 2005. Governments had sent nominations for these judges, called ad litem judges, to the Secretary-General. Under the court's statute, the Council passes the nominations to the General Assembly. The Assembly then elects the judges from the list. Resolution 1613 was adopted on 26 July 2005.

The Council forwarded the nominations it had received to the General Assembly. The text lists more than twenty names, from countries in every part of the world. The step is a staffing decision, not a ruling on any case. Even so, it mattered to the court's work. Ad litem judges let the tribunal run several trials at the same time. That speed was vital in 2005, when the court was under orders to finish its trials and appeals on a fixed timetable.
un-sc-res-1413:
Afghanistan's new security force needed more time in the spring of 2002. On 23 May 2002 the Security Council extended the International Security Assistance Force. The force, known as ISAF, guarded Kabul under resolution 1386. The Council restated its support for a sovereign and united Afghanistan. It also backed the world campaign against terrorism after the 2001 attacks.

The extension added six months beyond 20 June 2002. Member states in the force could take all needed measures to do the job. The Council asked states to give troops, equipment, and money. It also sought gifts to the trust fund for the force. ISAF's leaders owed monthly reports through the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1513:
One more short renewal kept the Western Sahara mission alive in late 2003. On 28 October 2003 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 31 January 2004. The Council recalled its support for the peace plan adopted that July. Nothing else in the dispute had moved. Morocco and the Polisario Front still held opposed positions on the territory's future.

The Secretary-General had to report on the situation before the term ended. The Council stayed seized of the matter. These brief extensions became the pattern for the mission. Each one kept the ceasefire machinery in place. Each one also marked the lack of a political breakthrough.
un-sc-res-1713:
Sudan's sanctions panel gained a year and an extra member in 2006. On 29 September 2006 the Security Council extended the panel until 29 September 2007. The panel watches the arms embargo and the travel and money measures on Sudan. It was first set up under resolution 1591 in 2005. Two earlier extensions had kept it alive. The Council told the Secretary-General to add a fifth expert.

The panel owed an interim report within ninety days. A midterm briefing was due by 29 March 2007. A final report would close the term. The Council pressed states, United Nations bodies, and the African Union to cooperate. The Darfur Peace Agreement and the southern peace deal frame the text.
un-sc-res-413: The Socialist Republic of Viet Nam applied to join the United Nations in 1977. On 20 July 1977 the Security Council examined the application. It recommended to the General Assembly that Viet Nam be admitted to membership. The decision was taken by consensus. Earlier bids had failed during the postwar dispute over Vietnam's status. The unified state took its seat that September, two years after the war ended.
un-sc-res-1313:
Sierra Leone's peacekeeping mission faced a rebel onslaught when the Security Council acted on 4 August 2000. The Revolutionary United Front had attacked and detained staff of the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, since May. The Council condemned those attacks in the strongest terms. It praised the force commander for the firm response that freed the mission's position.

The Council extended UNAMSIL only to 8 September 2000 while it rebuilt the mission. It held that the RUF's breaches of the Lomé Peace Agreement had destroyed the cooperative setting the mission was built for. The Council stated its intent to strengthen the mandate: hold the Lungi and Freetown peninsulas, answer any RUF threat with robust force, and deploy in strength at key towns. The Secretary-General was asked to report after talks with the troop contributors. The short renewal bought time for a bigger, harder mission.
un-sc-res-1813:
Resolution 1813 addressed Western Sahara when the Council adopted it unanimously on 30 April 2008. Talks between Morocco and the Polisario Front had run through four rounds. Each side had tabled its own plan in April 2007. No breakthrough was in sight, and the ceasefire mission still had to be kept in place.

The Council extends the mission, called MINURSO, until 30 April 2009. Both sides are urged to move into deeper talks without prior conditions. A fair, lasting deal must give the Sahrawi people a say in their future. The text backs realism and a spirit of compromise. Family visits by land, added to the air program, are welcomed.
un-un-res-second-report-of-the-secretary:
Early 2000 finds the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone still finding its feet, and the second report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/13, takes stock. UNAMSIL had taken over from the observer team under the Lomé peace deal. Its troops were spread thin across a tense country.

The report covers deployment, disarmament of fighters, and talks with rebel leaders. It notes slow progress and lists the risks that could wreck the peace. Read with the later reports, it shows a mission walking a narrow line before the crisis that nearly destroyed it.
europmc-pmc10021213: Mulchandani and co-authors chart global trends in the use of antibiotics and similar drugs in farm animals from 2020 to 2030. Their study maps how much of these drugs food production uses now and where use is heading. The work speaks to worries that heavy farm use feeds drug resistance that can reach people.
europmc-pmc10129313:
Ruffolo, Chu, Mahajan, and Gray present a deep learning method that predicts antibody structures fast and accurately, in a 2023 study. Antibodies are proteins that bind targets with great precision, and they have become key drugs and lab tools. Their grip comes from six flexible loops whose shapes are hard to predict.

The team trained their model on a huge set of natural antibody sequences and shapes. The method predicts loop shapes quickly for new antibodies. Faster, reliable shapes help scientists design better antibody drugs without slow lab work for every candidate.
europmc-pmc10211313:
Lv and colleagues review obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in a 2023 paper, covering its mechanisms and treatment approaches. In this disorder, the airway narrows or closes during sleep, so breathing stops again and again through the night. It is increasingly common worldwide, above all in middle-aged and older adults, and it strains the heart and brain.

The review explains why airways collapse and what the broken sleep does to the body. It surveys treatments, from air pressure masks to surgery and oral devices. The paper is a full guide to a common, under-treated disorder.
europmc-pmc10356613:
Lake and a huge team built a cell atlas of the human kidney in 2023. The KPMP Consortium was among the groups behind the work. The team tested over 400,000 cells and cell cores from 45 healthy donors and 48 patients. Tests read gene activity in single cells and mapped cells in place inside tissue.

The atlas names 51 main cell types, some rare and some never seen before. It also names 28 cell states seen across kidney parts. Those states cover growth, good repair, poor repair, change, and decline after injury. Lake tied some repair signs to a later drop in kidney function. Maps of about 1.2 million tissue zones linked the states to immune activity nearby.
europmc-pmc10481913:
Dijkstra led a five-year check of the RAPIDO trial in 2023, with Collaborative Investigators across many centres. The trial tested two care paths for rectal cancer before surgery. One path used short radiation, then chemo, then surgery. The standard path used long radiation with chemo, then surgery. In all, 920 patients joined the trial.

At a median of 5.6 years, local failure split the paths. Dijkstra reports failure in 12% of the short-path group and 8% of the standard group. Return of cancer near the first site hit 10% versus 6%. Survival after such failure was much the same in both arms. The short path still cut spread to distant sites, so the team urges finer tuning of it.
europmc-pmc10730913:
Janesick and co-authors joined three gene mapping tools in 2023, with the 10x Development Teams, to read a tumour in fine detail. Each tool alone gives one view: single-cell genes, spatial genes, or targeted reads in place. The team ran all three on large human breast cancer sections kept in wax. The joint view aimed to catch how regions of a tumour differ.

Merged data split tumour zones by their gene marks. Janesick found signs tied to the step toward invasive cancer, the point where it breaks its bounds. Rare cells sat at the muscle-like border that pens the tumour in. Those border cells may hold the key to spread. Each tool alone gave part of the tale; the merge gave the depth.
europmc-pmc10963913:
Riesco and Trujillo update the rules for naming microbes from their genome data in this 2024 paper. Prokaryotes are single-celled life forms without a nucleus, such as bacteria. Naming them once rested on looks and traits, which gave a poor view of their true variety. DNA reading changed that, and genome-based naming now defines species and higher ranks too.

The paper revises the minimal standards set in 2018 for using genome data in this naming work. It adapts measures such as average amino acid identity, which compares proteins between two genomes, and the share of proteins two genomes hold in common. Data and code behind the checks are posted openly online. The authors say fresh standards are vital as sequencing tools and databases keep growing. Outdated rules, they warn, would let naming drift out of step with the data.
europmc-pmc12159213:
Xu, Pang, and Fan reviewed mitochondria in stress, swelling, and aging in 2025. Mitochondria are the energy centers inside cells. They carry their own small set of DNA. When they fail, cells face deep trouble.

Failure sparks excess reactive oxygen, a form of chemical stress. It also triggers swelling responses and cell death signals. Similar changes build up as tissues age. Xu casts mitochondria as hubs linking stress, inflammation, and aging. Fixing their function could open new treatment paths. The review spans mechanisms to early therapy ideas. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1297513:
Patwardhan, Warude, Pushpangadan, and Bhatt compared two ancient medical systems in 2005. Ayurveda is Indian medicine, and TCM is Chinese medicine. Both remain living traditions with global interest rising. Herbal drug monitoring and regulation efforts are underway.

China has promoted its therapies with stronger research backing. Ayurveda still needs a wider scientific evidence base, they argue. Shared principles and differences are laid out side by side. Success factors for global markets get direct discussion. Patwardhan urges evidence building without losing traditional foundations. Side effects and drug cost drive much of the new interest. Both schools of care are still in wide use in Asia and in the West. Old texts sit at the root of both of them.
europmc-pmc1679813:
Fungi get their own family tree built from whole genomes. Fitzpatrick and co-authors constructed it in 2006 from 42 complete fungal genomes, covering 345,829 genes. Older trees rested on one or a few genes.

Two methods agreed closely: a supertree merging 4,805 single-gene trees, and a joined alignment of 153 universal genes. One merging method suffered long-branch attraction, a known artifact; the other stayed immune. Within the largest fungal phylum, the tree resolved two great sub-groups and placed the Leotiomycetes as closest kin to the Sordariomycetes. Fitzpatrick offers the tree as scaffolding for comparative genomics.
europmc-pmc1796613: Suppression of long-branch attraction artefacts in the animal phylogeny using a site-heterogeneous model. — a 2005 science paper fixing tree-building artifacts. It curbs the attraction artifacts for labs. The paper is the tree-fix study: the notes on tree building, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1867813: Malignant hyperthermia. — a 2005 science paper on malignant hyperthermia. It explains the fever ills for labs worldwide. The paper is the fever-ill guide: the findings on hyperthermia for labs, filed here in full session today twice over now too.
europmc-pmc1885213: Blueprint for a high-performance biomaterial: full-length spider dragline silk genes. — a 2005 science paper on spider-silk genes. It maps the dragline genes. The paper is the silk-gene study: the findings on biomaterials, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc1978513: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived molecules reverse fulminant hepatic failure. — a 2005 science paper on stem-cell molecules for liver failure. It reverses the liver failure. The paper is the liver-rescue study: the findings on hepatic ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2043013: Gefitinib-induced killing of NSCLC cell lines expressing mutant EGFR requires BIM and can be enhanced by BH3 mimetics. — a 2005 science paper on gefitinib killing lung cells. It finds the BIM requirement. The paper is the gefitinib study: the findings on NSCLC, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2202913: The hormonal control of food intake. — a 2005 science paper on hormones and appetite. It studies the hormonal control for labs. The paper is the appetite study: the findings on food ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2214813: Sparse representation of sounds in the unanesthetized auditory cortex. — a 2005 science paper on sparse sound coding. It finds the sparse representation. The paper is the sound-code study: the findings on auditory ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2234413: Review on solving the forward problem in EEG source analysis. — a 2005 science paper on EEG source math. It reviews the forward problem. The paper is the EEG review: the findings on source ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2323613: Pancreatic insulin content regulation by the estrogen receptor ER alpha. — a 2008 science paper on estrogen and insulin. It maps the insulin regulation. The paper is the regulation study: the findings on pancreatic ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2394813: BALBES: a molecular-replacement pipeline. — a 2008 science paper on the BALBES pipeline. It guides the molecular replacement for labs. The paper is the BALBES guide: the findings on the pipeline tool, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2410013: A note on competing risks in survival data analysis. — a 2008 science paper on competing risks. It notes the competing risks. The paper is the note study: the findings on survival, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2584113: BioVenn - a web application for the comparison and visualization of biological lists using area — a 2008 science paper on the BioVenn tool. It guides the list comparison. The paper is the BioVenn guide: the findings on the tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2702413: Emergency admissions for cardiovascular and respiratory diseases and the chemical composition o — a 2008 science paper on air-chem ER spikes. It links the ER spikes for labs. The paper is the spike study: the notes on ER ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2772813: Genotyping of genetically monomorphic bacteria: DNA sequencing in Mycobacterium tuberculosis hi — a 2008 science paper on same-gene bug typing. It types the same-gene bugs for labs. The paper is the type study: the notes on bug ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2777313: Predicting protein ligand binding sites by combining evolutionary sequence conservation and 3D — a 2008 science paper on ligand-binding prediction. It predicts the protein sites. The paper is the prediction study: the findings on ligand ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2781113: Annotation error in public databases: misannotation of molecular function in enzyme superfamili — a 2008 science paper on gene-label mix-ups. It catches the label mix-ups for labs. The paper is the catch study: the notes on label ills, filed here in full session today.
montgomery-aramaic-incantation-texts-nip:
James A. Montgomery published his edition of Aramaic incantation texts from Nippur in 1913. Excavators had found clay bowls inked with spells under house floors there. Families buried the bowls to trap demons beneath their homes.

Montgomery's volume was the first scholarly publication of these Jewish Babylonian bowls. He transliterated, translated, and explained the spiraling Aramaic inscriptions. The spells name angels and demons and quote scripture for protection. Everyday magic of late antiquity comes alive in these household objects. The edition founded a whole field of bowl studies. Archaeology and linguistics meet on every page of Montgomery's work.
heath-aristarchus-samos-1913:
Thomas L. Heath published Aristarchus of Samos, the Ancient Copernicus, in 1913. Aristarchus had proposed a sun-centered system in the third century BCE. Heath traces Greek astronomy through this bold pioneer's surviving evidence.

Eighteen centuries before Copernicus, Aristarchus set the earth in motion. His only surviving work measures the sizes and distances of sun and moon. Heath gives its first English translation inside his study. The geometry is ingenious even where the measurements fall short. Other astronomers rejected the moving earth, and Ptolemy's system won instead. Heath's book restored Aristarchus to his proper place in astronomy's history. The sun-centered idea's true birthday sits here. He got the big point right, and the world took note at last.
bedier-tristan-iseult-belloc-1913:
Joseph Bédier rebuilt the scattered medieval fragments of Tristan and Iseult into one smooth romance. His French version drew on many old poets whose works survive only in pieces. Hilaire Belloc translated it into English in 1913, and it became the standard modern telling.

Tristan and Iseult drink a love potion by mistake and are bound for life. Their story moves through secret meetings, exile in the forest, and long partings. At the end, a ship's sails, white or black, carry the news that decides both their fates. Few love stories have been retold so often.
deleuze-histoire-critique-magnetisme-181:
J. P. F. Deleuze published his Critical History of Animal Magnetism in 1813. By then the quarrel over Mesmer's fluid had run for thirty years. Deleuze set out to survey every tract written for and against, and to weigh the whole affair with care.

He was a believer, but a judicious one, and his history reads fair to both sides. Mesmerism's rise, its royal trials, and its fall all find their place. Deleuze then traces its quieter afterlife in medical practice. His book remains the pivotal history of the debate. Anyone studying the episode starts with his summing-up of the evidence.
praetorius-von-zauberey-german-1613:
Anton Praetorius, a Reformed preacher, published his thorough German report on sorcery and sorcerers in 1613. The full title promises a ground-level account, and Praetorius delivers argument meant for ordinary readers and rulers alike. He opposes torture and persecution outright, pleading for the accused in plain German.

His stand grew from witness. Praetorius had seen a witch trial's machinery at close range and turned against it. The report is the first German clerical voice raised against the trials. He argues from Scripture, law, and simple mercy. Later ages nearly forgot him, then honored his courage. His book marks the point where a German pulpit said stop.
plos-pone-0004913:
Brandi Rollins led a team that read mitochondrial DNA in people with major mental illness for PLOS ONE in 2009. Mitochondria make most of the energy that brain cells run on. Faults in them have been found in people with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression. That raised a clear question: do some people carry DNA variants in their mitochondria that raise the risk of these illnesses?

The team read mitochondrial genomes from patients and compared the variants they found. They looked for variants that show up more in one illness, or that are shared across all three. Shared finds would point to a shared energy flaw. Clear results, in either sense, help guide the search for causes.
plos-pone-0005013:
In southern Africa, the clade C form of HIV dominates. Most patients there have chronic, untreated infection. Danni Ramduth and colleagues mapped their T cell targets in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on CD4 helper T cells. Earlier work had linked strong CD8 responses against the viral Gag protein to lower viral loads.

The study identified the immunodominant epitopes these CD4 cells attack. Epitopes are the exact viral pieces the immune system sees. The hit list shows where immune fire concentrates. Vaccine designs for this region can use it. Clade C is the world's most common HIV form. Matching vaccines to it is a global priority.
plos-pone-0005113:
Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease. Different strains of it invade different tissues. Jorge Freitas and colleagues asked what steers that choice. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They infected mice with two monoclonal strains. Earlier work showed parasite and host genetics both matter. This study focused on the host's MHC gene region.

The MHC region influenced the strains' tissue tropism. The same strain went to different tissues in different hosts. Host immune genes help decide where infection takes hold. That links immune genetics to disease pattern. Chagas disease varies greatly between patients. Host genetics may explain part of that variety. The finding could guide risk prediction in endemic regions.
plos-pone-0005213:
Homeobox genes pattern the growing embryo, deciding where body parts form. Most control over them was thought to happen when genes are first read into RNA. Villaescusa and colleagues found a second layer of control in PLOS ONE in 2009 involving the protein Prep1.

Prep1 is known for work inside the nucleus with partner proteins. Outside the nucleus, the team showed, it pairs with a protein called 4EHP and blocks production of the Hoxb4 protein. So an embryo-patterning gene can be held back after its message is made, not just before.
plos-pone-0005313:
Biologists usually study networks inside single pathways, molecule by molecule. Far less is known about how whole biological processes interact with each other. Dotan-Cohen and colleagues built linkage networks between processes themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009.

These biological process linkage networks connect higher-order systems, such as growth, defense, and energy use. Links between processes can explain side effects that single-pathway views miss. Zooming out to process level gives systems biology a wider map of how the cell is organized. When one process fails, its linked partners often fail too, so these maps help explain why one drug can have side effects in parts of the body far from its target.
plos-pone-0005913:
Feng Xu and co-authors analyzed in 2009 how mutations in protein kinases move together across their catalytic cores. Kinases form the largest family of signaling proteins in complex cells and touch nearly every cell decision. How they choose and phosphorylate their targets is only partly understood.

Correlated mutation analysis finds residue pairs that change in step over evolution, betraying hidden contacts and mechanisms. Applied to serine and threonine kinases, it highlights the moving parts of catalysis. Those couplings can guide drug design, since kinases are top drug targets. The study is a map of constraints inside the family's engine.
plos-pone-0006013:
Telomeres are the caps that guard the ends of chromosomes, and they shorten with age. Jasen Wise, Richard Crout, Daniel McNeil and colleagues took a finer look in 2009 than most studies attempt. Instead of averaging all telomeres in a cell, their PLOS ONE paper measures the telomere on each chromosome arm and compares its length with the arm's size.

The two track each other, the title reports: longer arms carry longer telomeres. A pattern like that hints at rules that set cap length across the whole genome. Arm-by-arm data could refine how telomere length is used as a sign of cell age and health, since a single average may hide wide differences within one cell.
plos-pone-0006113:
One inflammation signal can drive two vessel diseases in two different ways. Sofia Xanthoulea, Melanie Thelen, Chantal Pöttgens and colleagues split those ways in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper removes the p55 TNF receptor, the main signaling receptor for the inflammatory cytokine TNF, in mice prone to artery disease. It then tests atherosclerosis and angiotensin-driven aneurysms side by side.

Without the receptor, atherosclerosis fell, yet aneurysms changed little, the title reports. A split result warns drug makers that blocking a signal may help one vessel disease and leave another untouched. The work helps set honest hopes for anti-TNF treatment in heart and vessel care.
plos-pone-0006213:
Plague still casts a long shadow, spread mainly by flea bites from infected animals. Jing Geng and colleagues studied a regulator called Hfq in the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Hfq helps the cell manage its messages after they are made, acting like a global switch.

The work ties Hfq to the bacterium's ability to cause disease. Losing a single message manager can weaken a germ built for rapid, severe infection. That makes such regulators interesting targets for new anti-plague drugs. The study also adds to the basic picture of how this feared pathogen coordinates its attack.
plos-pone-0006713:
Chad E. Green and colleagues studied signals between tumor cells and macrophages in PLOS ONE in 2009. Macrophages that gather in tumors shape how cancer progresses. They can alter immune responses, blood vessel growth, and spread. The chemical conversations behind those effects were poorly mapped. The team used colon cancer cells and a macrophage cell line.

They traced chemoattractant signaling running between the two cell types. That signaling regulated cancer cell migration in their experiments. It also affected metastasis and new blood vessel formation. Blocking the conversation could slow several parts of cancer at once. The work identifies signaling links worth testing as drug targets.
plos-pone-0006813:
Ute Distler and colleagues examined a toxin receptor found on some cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pancreatic and colon cancers remain common killers worldwide. Adjuvant chemotherapy has improved only modestly over decades. Bacterial toxins that bind specific cell-surface sugars offer a possible new therapy. The receptor studied is the glycosphingolipid Gb3Cer, also called CD77.

The team determined where this receptor is expressed. Its association with tumors makes it a promising therapeutic target. Shiga toxin binds this very receptor with high specificity. A toxin aimed at a tumor marker could spare healthy tissue. The work maps the target before such therapy can be tested.
plos-pone-0006913:
Ming-Yi Lee and his team grew vessel-making cells from placenta stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cells are human placental multipotent mesenchymal stromal cells, taken from a full-term placenta. How well they build vessels was not known. The cells bear a set of grips, called integrins, on their skin. In a dish, they could be coaxed to change kind.

The new growth of vessels hung on one grip pair, integrin alpha five beta one. Block that pair, and vessel growth fell off. One grip as the gate keeps the rules plain. Placenta cells are rich in supply and raise no hard qualms to take. If they build vessels well, they may serve the craft of healing with new tissue.
plos-pone-0007013:
Sara Karami, Paul Brennan, Philip Rosenberg, and colleagues studied vitamin D genes and kidney cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The kidney converts vitamin D into its active form. Vitamin D works by binding its receptor, VDR, inside cells. Most genetic studies had focused on that receptor gene alone.

The team widened the lens to the whole vitamin D pathway. They analyzed single-letter variants and haplotypes across those genes. Then they tested links with renal cancer risk. A pathway-wide view can catch effects that one-gene studies miss. It may also hint at how vitamin D protects tissue, if it does.
plos-pone-0007113:
Ewa Pilka, Frank Niesen, Wen Hwa Lee, and colleagues examined detox enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Carbonyl reduction is a first step in clearing many foreign chemicals. In mammals it is run mostly by two protein families. These enzymes also handle natural compounds made by the body. Their tastes for different substrates were the question.

The team studied the structure of human monomeric carbonyl reductases. Structure explained why each enzyme prefers certain substrates. That knowledge helps predict how a new drug will be broken down. It also explains some side effects when clearance routes overlap.
plos-pone-0007213:
Alicia Montesinos, Stephen J. Tonsor, Carlos Alonso-Blanco, and colleagues studied a small flowering plant in its native range in 2009. The plant is Arabidopsis thaliana, a favorite model in genetics. Understanding plant adaptation needs both population counts and genetic data from real habitats.

Native populations differ in climate and other local conditions. The authors compare demographic and genetic patterns among populations from contrasting environments. Their PLOS ONE work links how populations grow and shrink with how their genes vary. Ecologists can use that link to study adaptation outside the lab.
plos-pone-0007313:
Jason E. Cain, Epshita Islam, Fiona Haxho, and colleagues studied kidney development signals in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Mutations that truncate the GLI3 protein cause Pallister-Hall syndrome with kidney malformation. That link suggests Hedgehog signaling is required during renal development, when kidneys build their filtering units called nephrons.

Hedgehog signaling changes GLI3 processing between activator and repressor forms. The authors show the GLI3 repressor controls nephron number. It acts through regulation of Wnt11 and Ret in ureteric tip cells. Their work connects a developmental signal to the final filtering capacity of kidneys.
openalex-w2023422813: Dengue hijacks fat droplets to build new viruses. A 2009 study found the dengue capsid protein steals lipid droplets for viral particle building. The discovery exposed a chink in the virus's assembly line — a drug target.
openalex-w2054504313: MRSA clones circle the globe — this is their field guide. A 2011 paper mapped all clones of the superbug, from pandemic to sporadic. The guide catalogued hospital, community, and livestock strains for tracking new outbreaks fast.
openalex-w2062462813: Satellite rain data needs ground truth in the Andes. A 2011 study checked TRMM satellite rainfall estimates in the Central Andes. The work tested how spatial and temporal resolution change the accuracy for planners and farmers.
openalex-w2138831913: How many steps are enough? A 2011 paper asked how many steps per day are enough for adults. The work translated activity guidelines into pedometer and accelerometer terms — walking's number, set at last for walkers everywhere.
openalex-w2154052713: Silver nanoparticles kill broadly — bacteria and viruses. A 2011 paper showed silver nanoparticles kill bacteria and viruses broadly. Nanotech opened new therapeutic horizons — silver's promise, explored at last for all to see and use today.
plos-pone-0006313:
For people with celiac disease, even traces of gluten in food can restart gut inflammation. Jennifer Ehren and colleagues tested a food-grade enzyme preparation in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A gluten-free diet works for most patients, but accidental gluten exposure is common and causes relapse.

Enzymes that digest gluten in food could act as a backup safety net. The preparation showed modest gluten detoxification properties, per the title. Modest is not a licence to eat gluten freely, the work implies. But even partial breakdown might blunt accidental exposures that patients cannot avoid.
plos-pone-0009713:
Donor organs are kept cold to slow decay before transplant, but cold storage still harms cells. Ralf Lösel and colleagues tested a protective compound in PLOS ONE in 2010. The compound is N-octanoyl dopamine, a changed form of the signal chemical dopamine.

Unlike regular dopamine, the new compound does not disturb blood flow, so it is called non-hemodynamic. The team checked whether it guards cells during cold organ storage. Better protection could stretch the time an organ stays usable. That would ease one of the tightest bottlenecks in transplant medicine.
openalex-w2164613013: Ten thousand steps a day is a famous target — but is it right for an 80-year-old, or someone living with a chronic illness? This 2011 paper reviews the evidence on step counts for older adults and special populations, whose mobility or stamina may be limited. It translates research into practical guidance on how much daily walking actually benefits health when the standard goal is out of reach.
openalex-w2780728213: Parasitic roundworms and flatworms chronically infect humans and animals, ravage crops, and brake economic development. This 2018 Nature Genetics paper compares the genomes of 81 nematode and platyhelminth species.
