The genomic contrasts reveal how parasites evolved their stealthy lifestyles — and where their biology might be vulnerable.
openalex-w4385691013: Twenty-five years after landmark ecosystem-service valuations, biodiversity decisions still ignore nature’s diverse values. This 2023 Nature paper confronts the barriers to incorporating those values into decision-making. The analysis aims to break the impasse blocking conservation.
openalex-w4406161213: Freshwater ecosystems are biodiverse and economically vital — and under severe stress. This 2025 Nature paper finds one-quarter of freshwater fauna threatened with extinction: the first comprehensive global assessment for these speciose groups. The verdict is alarming.
europmc-pmc2807913: Plants sense drought through the hormone abscisic acid, and this 2010 paper fills in a missing link in that chain. The authors identify PYR/PYL/RCAR family proteins as the main partners of the ABI1 phosphatase inside living Arabidopsis cells. Pinning down these interactions clarifies how the drought signal gets through. The finding advanced efforts to breed more drought-tolerant crops.
europmc-pmc2826413: The Parkinson's-tied protein DJ-1 guards the cell's power packs. This 2010 paper shows that losing DJ-1 cuts the cell's self-cleaning and wrecks power-pack upkeep. The team traces how its loss lets harm pile up. The work ties one gene to the cell faults behind Parkinson's.
europmc-pmc2831913: Air pollution does not hit men and women identically. This 2010 paper argues for a growing role of gender analysis in air pollution epidemiology. The author reviews why sex and gender matter in exposure and health effects. The call pushed researchers to stop treating gender as an afterthought in pollution studies.
europmc-pmc2852313: Coot lets researchers build and fix protein models by hand on screen, turning raw X-ray data into finished structures. This 2010 paper tours the tool's traits and growth, from its first release to wide adoption. The authors chart how it won its users with speed and a friendly design. The write-up marks the rise of a lab staple that many crystallographers still open daily.
europmc-pmc2855713: Green tea compounds are tested against cancer cells with color-change assays, but this 2010 paper warns the tests can lie. The authors show MTT and MTS assays misread the anti-growth effects of green tea polyphenols. Their caution matters because false readings waste research. The paper taught tea researchers to distrust a popular shortcut.
europmc-pmc2891813: Malaria persists in Brazil's vast terrain, and this 2010 paper surveys the fight. The authors give an overview of malaria in Brazil, its patterns and control. Their synthesis aids a large country's campaign. The review is a reference for Latin American malaria.
europmc-pmc2930213: White blood cells live fast and die young, and this 2010 review tracks them. The authors cover neutrophil life cycles in health and disease. Their overview follows the short, fierce life of a front-line defender. The review helps doctors read immune cell counts.
europmc-pmc2936113: Memory runs on brain highways, and this 2010 paper maps two key ones. The authors uncover direct and indirect pathways linking the hippocampus to the anterior thalamus for memory. Their wiring diagram explains how recall travels. The work guides memory research and its disorders.
europmc-pmc2936313: The pregnancy hormone hCG does more than turn tests positive. This 2010 review covers the many jobs of hCG and its kin molecules in the body. The author's tour spans womb, ovary, and beyond. Their review clarifies what a famous hormone really does.
europmc-pmc3000813: Blood chemistry mirrors blood sugar control. This 2010 study charts blood chemistry in obese Black women with and without diabetes. The authors reveal the metabolic signature. Their work points to early markers. The signature differs sharply between the groups. Doctors may spot risk before sugar spikes.
europmc-pmc3017113: Insect-killing fungi got their genomes read. This 2011 paper sequences two Metarhizium fungi and compares their active genes. The authors reveal the killers' toolkit. Their work aids green pesticides. The fungi punch through insect armor. Farmers spray spores instead of chemicals.
europmc-pmc3053313: The brain learns from movement mistakes. This 2011 paper shows the brain uses surprise signals to tune reaching movements. The authors reveal the error codes. Their work informs robots and rehab. Reward sweetens the learning signal. Stroke patients relearn reach with these cues.
europmc-pmc3156713: Schoolkids' face time got measured. This 2011 paper tracks face-to-face contact patterns in a primary school. The authors map the mixing. Their work guides outbreak models. Kids mixed most at lunch, they found. Closing schools cut contacts sharply. The data powered flu simulations.
europmc-pmc3228813: The genome's repeats got bigger. This 2011 paper argues repeats may fill over two-thirds of the human genome. The authors revise the count upward. Their work reshaped genomics. Old estimates said half, they show. The repeats shape evolution, they argue.
europmc-pmc3270013: Sequencing data got a QC toolkit. This 2012 paper brings a toolkit for checking next-gen sequencing data quality. The authors' tool cleans the data. Their software spread through labs. Indian labs built and shared it. The toolkit is open source.
europmc-pmc3356313: COPD got an inflammation warning. This 2012 paper links lasting inflammation to poor COPD outcomes. The authors reveal the pattern. Their work guides treatment. Agustí's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped COPD care. The study is a classic.
europmc-pmc3418213: Diabetes classes got a group-test review. This 2012 review tests group diabetes classes vs routine care. The authors reveal the benefit. Their work guides clinics. Steinsbekk's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. Groups won, they found. It shaped clinic programs.
europmc-pmc3473013: High-fat diet got a gut-germ inflammation. This 2012 paper shows high-fat diet gut germs worsen inflammation via TLR4. The authors reveal the pathway. Their work guides research. Kim's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3486913: C. diff got a defined germ cocktail. This 2012 paper cures relapsing C. difficile in mice with defined germs. The authors reveal the cure. Their work points to therapy. Lawley's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3509513: Green tea got an EGCG cancer review. This 2012 paper reviews EGCG, green tea's top cancer-fighting compound. The authors weigh the evidence. Their overview guides nutrition. Du's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped tea research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3560213: Cells got an electric monitor. This 2013 paper reviews electric cell monitoring for barrier tests. The authors map the uses. Their review guides bioengineering. Benson's review is widely cited. It is a classic. Labs adopted the method. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3570213: C9orf72 got a structural link. This 2013 paper links the C9orf72 protein to DENN Rab-GEFs. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides brain-disease research. Levine's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped ALS genetics.
europmc-pmc3605113: Risk scores got a power analysis. This 2013 paper tests how accurate gene-based risk scores are. The author reveals the power. Their work guides genetics. Dudbridge's paper is a classic. The paper is widely cited. It shaped genetic testing. It is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3652713: Chronic conditions got a counting framework. This 2013 paper defines and measures chronic conditions. The authors set research imperatives. Their work guides policy. Goodman's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped health statistics.
europmc-pmc3662313: Pompe disease got a TFEB target. This 2013 paper names TFEB as a Pompe disease target. The authors reveal the target. Their work guides therapy. Spampanato's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped Pompe therapy.
europmc-pmc3688513: Genomes got a hidden-RNAs study. This 2013 paper finds thousands of hidden long RNAs. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides genetics. Hangauer's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3692113: Genes got GeneMANIA 2013. This 2013 paper refreshes the GeneMANIA prediction server. The authors reveal the refresh. Their work spread through labs. Zuberi's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide. The study shaped gene networks.
europmc-pmc3695013: Brains got BrainAGE. This 2013 paper predicts Alzheimer's conversion with BrainAGE. The authors reveal the prediction. Their work guides neurology. Gaser's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped Alzheimer's tests. Clinics study it.
europmc-pmc3695513: Searches got an HMMER3-challenges paper. This 2013 paper covers protein-search challenges. The authors reveal the challenges. Their work guides bioinformaticians. Mistry's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Labs rely on it. It is open access.
europmc-pmc3699713: Colon cancer got PICCOLO. This 2013 trial tests panitumumab plus irinotecan. The authors reveal the results. Their work guides oncology. Seymour's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped colon-cancer drugs. Oncologists rely on it.
europmc-pmc3737713: Stress got a brain-control review. This 2013 paper reviews brain control of stress adaptation. The author maps the control. Their review guides neuroscience. Herman's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped stress research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3752613: HIV got a CRISPR-attack study. This 2013 paper uses CRISPR to attack hidden HIV. The authors reveal the attack. Their work guides cure research. Ebina's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped HIV cure science.
europmc-pmc3764313: Patients got a health-survey shootout. This 2013 study compares two health surveys. The authors reveal the winner. Their work guides health economics. Janssen's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped health measures.
europmc-pmc3781313: Immunity got a white-cell brake review. This 2013 paper reviews white-cell braking of immunity. The authors map the brakes. Their review guides immunology. Pillay's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer immunology. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3800813: Brains got a brain-zap focus review. This 2013 paper reviews why brain zaps hit targets. The authors map the reasons. Their review guides neuroscience. Bikson's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped brain stimulation. The review is widely taught.

The Youth's Companion was America's best-loved family weekly for a hundred years. This number, volume 52 number 11, is dated Thursday, March 13, 1879. J. T. Trowbridge, a regular contributor, supplies the lead story. In it a one-eyed hostler leans on a bar and lectures on bears. Let them alone, he says, and they will mostly let you alone. A vicious one turns up now and then.

Stories, poems, household pages, and a children's corner fill the issue. The Companion reached more American homes than any magazine of its century. Mark Twain and a dozen presidents wrote for it. One surviving number shows the wholesome, story-rich mixture that made it a fixture by the fireside.
arxiv-2601-08113: Nardos Belay Abera and Yize Chen study how to run AI data centers with less energy and carbon cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that such centers are being built at large scale for large language models. Christian Bar proves an upper bound for total mean curvature of spin fill-ins in 2026. Gromov conjectured such an estimate for compact Riemannian manifolds. The bound should depend only on the boundary metric, Gromov proposed.

It should also depend on a lower bound for the fill-in's scalar curvature. Bar proves Gromov's conjecture when the manifolds are spin. He also assumes the mean curvature H is non-negative throughout. Total mean curvature measures how the boundary bends on average everywhere. Bounding it from boundary data alone is a strong rigidity statement. geometers working on scalar curvature will use this result directly. Spin geometry here delivers what general methods could not yet. The proof closes a named conjecture in a natural class.
arxiv-2601-07713:
Jules Linden, Cathal O'Donoghue, and Denisa Sologon review what is known about who bears the cost of carbon taxes. Carbon taxes are popular with policymakers but politically contentious. The central dispute is distributional: burdens differ across population groups. Poorer households often spend a larger share of income on energy. The authors' 2026 preprint is a systematic review and meta-analysis of modeling studies.

Most studies assess the impact in advance using microsimulation models. A meta-analysis pools their results to find consistent patterns. Knowing which groups lose, and by how much, shapes compensation design. Revenue recycling can offset burdens if it is aimed well. The review serves policymakers and economists who must judge fairness claims with evidence rather than slogans.
arxiv-2601-07913:
Dmitry Shishkin and Amir Michaelis measure symmetry in pictures of exploded stars and glowing gas shells. They present a pipeline based on Transformation Information, an information measure of self-similarity under geometric changes. The measure compares an image with its rotated or reflected copy on their overlap. The comparison uses a Kullback-Leibler divergence, expressed as cross-entropy. Their 2026 preprint applies the method to planetary nebulae and supernova remnants.

Symmetry in these objects records how the explosion or outflow was shaped. Eyeball judgments of symmetry are hard to reproduce. A number lets astronomers compare many objects on one scale. The pipeline is released as code, built on standard scientific Python tools. The paper serves astronomers studying stellar deaths. It turns a qualitative impression into a measurement.
arxiv-2601-07113:
Natham Aguirre wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the long-run values of a math model of training. The model comes from discrimination training, where a subject learns to tell two cues apart. Its core is a periodic linear difference equation. A difference equation gives the next value from past values, step by step.

The trait here is written w of t. The key term is w at a whole count of steps, each of length T. Aguirre asks what that term tends to as the count grows with no bound. The change in w at each step is set by two time-based terms. One is a drive term, F of t. The other is a loss term, A of t times w. The paper works out the end values the trait can reach. They tell what the model says a trained subject does in the long run.
arxiv-2601-08913:
Ambuj and four co-authors show a gain when a noisy plain link and a pure quantum link are used as a pair. Each link on its own can send a fixed count of notes with no flaw at all. One would guess the pair can send at most the product of those counts. The team shows that guess is wrong, in a good way.

Used as a pair, the links can send more flaw free notes than the product allows. The gain is called superadditivity. It means joint use beats the sum of parts in a strict sense. A reader in comms work gets a clean proof of that gain. It hints that mixed plain and quantum links may carry more than we thought.
arxiv-2601-09013:
James Wheeler couples a spin field to a broad form of gravity where the grid itself can twist and stretch. In that form, space is set by a frame that need not stay square or fixed in length. Twist is called torsion. Stretch of the grid is called nonmetricity. Both need a source, just as mass sources plain gravity.

Wheeler uses a Dirac field, the field for spin half bits like electrons, as that source. He ties the grid group to known spin groups by a clean map. That map lets the spin field drive twist in a direct way. A reader in gravity theory gets a neat source plan for two hard to source traits.
arxiv-2601-09813:
James W. G. Doran and four co-authors simulate tuberculosis spread in Uganda, person by person. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses agent-based modelling to study how gender shapes transmission. Tuberculosis is an airborne disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

In 2023, TB again became the world's leading killer among infectious diseases, passing COVID-19. More than ten million people are diagnosed each year. Men and women differ in exposure, care seeking, and risk, and a population average hides those gaps. An agent model can test which gender-linked factors drive the burden, guiding fairer control programs.
arxiv-2601-10013:
Ce Zheng, Shiyao Ma, Ke Zhang, Chen Sun, and Wenqi Zhang pick which users train a shared model. In shared training, phones train one model with no raw data sent. But tests of this work often split data in ways no real net would see.

Phone data also link to each other in real nets. Past picks for who trains next tend to miss those links. The team made a pick plan that uses side facts about users. It groups users by those facts first. The plan is built for real phone nets run to 3GPP rules. It aims for picks that match how data truly splits.
arxiv-2601-10313:
Peng-Fei Zhang and Zi Huang build attacks that can fool many sight and text models at once. A small change to an image can flip a model's call. Such tests show how frail a model is. Past attacks were made for one case at a time. That makes them slow to run at scale.

A broad attack works on new cases with no fresh build. The team refine such attacks in stages. Each stage hones the change for a wider set of cases. The aim is a cheap, broad test of model frailty. Labs can then rank models by how well they stand up.
arxiv-2601-10413:
Haiyue Yuan, Nikolay Matyunin, Ali Raza, and Shujun Li map how firms move user data, from their own privacy texts. Such texts state what data is took, kept, and shared. But they are long and dense with law terms. Few users can read them in full. Firms also phrase like facts in unlike ways.

The team built LADFA to read these texts at scale. It pairs a large language model with fetched facts. It pulls out the flow of user data: what, to whom, and why. The map can then be checked by pros. It makes a firm's true flow clear to see.
arxiv-2601-10513:
Xuan Luo and co authors test how well large omni models show empathy. Such models take in text, sound, and sight at once. To judge them on their own is a key need. But empathy is a feel trait. It is hard to score by a fixed rule.

The team built AEQ-Bench for this task. It grades how a model reads and meets the moods of a user. Cues may come in words, tone, or face. The bench joins all three. It gives a shared scale for a trait that past tests split by mode. That helps labs rank omni models on care, not just facts.
arxiv-2601-10813:
Srivathsan Poyyapakkam Sundar, Vibin Abraham, Bo Peng, and Ayush Asthana set out benchmarks meant to be decisive for quantum chemistry. Progress toward quantum utility needs more than better algorithms. It needs chemical problems whose electronic structure truly strains classical methods. Only then can a quantum machine prove its worth on a task that matters.

The authors curate a hierarchy of such benchmark systems. The sets probe distinct regimes of electron correlation. They span molecular, bioinorganic, and heavy-element chemistry. A shared ladder of hard cases lets teams compare machines and methods fairly. It also keeps the field honest about where quantum advantage is real and where it is still a hope.
arxiv-2601-10913:
Santiago Martínez Novoa, María Catalina Ibáñez, Lina Gómez Mesa, and Jeremias Kramer survey methods for classifying chest X-ray diseases. Chest X-rays are among the most common scans used to diagnose diseases of the thorax. Reading them at scale is slow, skilled work. The authors review several image processing and analysis techniques for the multi-class task.

Among the methods covered is DenseNet121, a deep network widely used for medical images. The team also deploys an open-source web application that puts the classifier to use. A browser tool can bring automated reading to clinics without local AI hardware. The work serves both researchers comparing methods and practitioners who need working tools.
arxiv-2601-11113:
Lele Zheng and co-authors fine-tune large language models in a subspace under differential privacy. Fine-tuning adapts a model to a task, often on sensitive data. Differential privacy gives strict guarantees, but adding noise across the full parameter space creates huge perturbations. Training wobbles and quality drops. The authors confine the noise to a subspace instead.

Working in a lower-dimensional subspace shrinks the noise's total size. Privacy guarantees can hold while the model still learns. The balance matters for hospitals, law firms, and banks that fine-tune on private records. The work offers a steadier path to private adaptation than naive noise over billions of parameters.
arxiv-2601-12013:
Hollis Williams runs a numeric study of Hawking mass for closed surfaces moved by expanding flows. The surfaces sit in flat Minkowski spacetime and are not spheres. Under smooth flow, Hawking mass should rise in a set way in the curved case.

Less is known when that flow is run by discrete code on set shapes far from round. His tests check if the rise still holds in such code. That check matters for numeric work in gravity, where code must track theory. It shows where discrete flows can be trusted.
arxiv-2601-12213:
Hongyang R. Zhang, Zhenshuo Zhang, Huy L. Nguyen, and Guanghui Lan revisit matrix completion when samples are ultra-sparse. Matrix completion fills a table from a few seen cells. In their case, each cell is seen with low chance. The chance is C over d, for a fixed whole number C of at least two.

That is far fewer samples than most past work assumes. The team ask what can still be recovered in that regime. Ultra-sparse results matter for surveys and sensor nets where each cell is costly. The work sets new limits for the task.
arxiv-2601-11713:
Rodney Martinez Alonso and four coauthors reject interference with wireless autoencoders. Their 2026 preprint works in the Walsh domain for ultrawideband links. Inter-cell interference can swamp a receiver in dense networks. Partial in-band interference is the specific foe here.

Narrower-band 5G base stations coexist with the UWB system. Their signals leak into the band and jam reception. The team designs an end-to-end wireless autoencoder. Transmitter and receiver are jointly optimized as one net. The encoding and decoding run in the Walsh domain. Walsh structure can spread signals away from the jammer. The method aims to keep links live amid interference.
arxiv-2601-13013:
Xiaohui Zhao, Xinjian Zhao, and co-authors tackle a key task for news feed ads at Baidu. The task is to guess the long term worth of each user to the firm. Good guesses help set bids and split funds for growth over time, not just quick clicks.

The team names two blocks in the way. First, ads aimed by age or group traits give worth values that swing a lot across groups. Second, fast shifts in ad plans make user act chains uneven, and tastes change fast. Their answer is a graph based net that tracks both links and time. The name joins hyper graph links with time steps to catch both effects at once.
arxiv-2601-13113:
Di Wang and Fa-Yin Wang model what happens when a giant star strays near a huge black hole. As the star nears, tides shake it and drain energy from its orbit. That drain can trap the star in orbit around the hole, a path called tidal capture.

If the star strays closer still, tides can tear off part of it. Such a partial tear can then repeat on later passes. The pair model how capture and repeat tears link to each other. Their work helps read brief bright flares seen in far galaxy cores. It also helps guess how often such repeat events should turn up in sky surveys.
arxiv-2601-13513:
Noriyuki Tonami and co-authors sort sound events when many mics in a spread array are marred. Spread multi channel sound sense can tag events at large scale, from street noise to faults. Its score drops when many channels are worn. It drops too when the test layout parts from the train layout.

Their front end paints in the lost parts by physics, with no learn step. It uses reverse time migration, a wave back track tool from geophysics. That paint step feeds a stock event tagger. A learn free front end can be set on a new array with no re teach. For sound teams, that ease is the gain.
arxiv-2601-12413:
Shihong Liu and nine co authors work on how to measure oxygen in far off galaxies. Telescopes like JWST now let us probe galaxies at high redshift. A key value is oxygen abundance, which tracks how enriched a galaxy is. Common tools for this task use strong spectral lines, with names like O3N2 and R23.

The team show that these tools lose precision at high redshift. At a fixed oxygen level, galaxies span a wide range in other traits. Ionization level and nitrogen enrichment both shift a lot from galaxy to galaxy. That spread blurs the line based estimates. Their work updates the diagnostics to deal with this spread and give sharper values.
arxiv-2601-12513:
Barbara Siljeg and six co authors image a galaxy that was thought to be dark. Dark galaxies hold lots of neutral hydrogen gas but no stars, or so the label claims. Models and simulations predict such systems should be common. Yet firm cases in hydrogen surveys have been hard to pin down, since a starless cloud is easy to doubt.

The team take high resolution hydrogen images of one candidate, J0139+4328. Their title gives the twist: the galaxy is not so dark after all. They identify an optical counterpart, faint starlight at the same spot. A case like this sharpens the hunt for truly dark galaxies. It shows how deep imaging can reclassify a supposed dark system.
arxiv-2601-12613:
Nathan Lindzey proves an Eventown style result for permutations. Eventown problems ask how large a family can be when all its members meet each other in a set way. Here the family consists of permutations of n elements. The meeting rule is that the ratio of any two members must contain an even cycle.

That rule is called even cycle intersecting in the work. Lindzey finds how large such a family can be, in the spirit of the classic Eventown theorem. Extremal results like this are gems of combinatorics. They often come with rigid structure for the largest families. The permutation setting links the problem to the symmetric group, a hub of algebra.
arxiv-2601-12813:
Keyin Wang and six co authors present a formally verified procedure for width inference in FIRRTL. FIRRTL is an intermediate language for register transfer level hardware designs. Bit widths of many components are not stated explicitly in FIRRTL programs. Compilers must infer those widths during compilation, a step called InferWidths.

The official compiler pass can fail even for simple FIRRTL programs. A verified procedure would rule out such failures by proof, not by testing. Formal verification checks the inference logic against a precise specification. Hardware bugs are costly, so compiler correctness matters from the first pass. The work was supported by Chinese research programs.
arxiv-2601-12913:
Pietro Barbiero and six co authors argue that the study of AI interpretability needs a new base. In their view, the field is ill posed as it now stands. The word itself has no test that can say if a method works. A term that cannot be tested cannot guide design, they argue.

They hold that a useful sense of the word must rest on symmetries. A symmetry is a change that leaves the key facts the same. Such rules can shape how a model is built and can be checked. Theirs is a position paper, a call to reset the terms of a field. It speaks to teams who build and judge tools that explain AI.
arxiv-2601-13713:
Aditya Bharat Soni and co-authors train open models to write tests that replay reported bugs in 2026. A good reproduction test shows a bug in code from a plain-language issue report. Such tests help devs find the root cause fast. They also back test-first work, where the test comes before the fix.

Their system, SWE-Tester, trains open-source language models for this task. It works on real-world code stores, not toy examples. Better bug replay tests can also make coding agents more effective. The work targets a slow, manual step in daily software work.
arxiv-2601-14413:
Matheus Curado Ferreira, F. T. Falciano, and Guilherme L. Pimentel mix two inflation ideas in this 2026 paper. Ghost inflation is a known framework where cosmological fluctuations can generate enhanced primordial non-Gaussianity, mostly of the equilateral type. In its original form, it clashes with current observational constraints. The team tries a distinct setup.

In their model, a standard inflaton drives the background expansion. Excitations of a ghost condensate act as spectator fields that interact with the inflaton. The title calls this amplifying the cosmological collider. That phrase names the hunt for particle marks in the pattern of primordial fluctuations. The work is pure theory. It adds no new sky data, but it does add a new test for old data. Readers get a new route to strong signals that past ghost models could not keep.
arxiv-2601-14813:
Jule Schindler and Emil Wiedemann study a fluid model in this 2026 math paper. The inviscid Leray-alpha equations are an inviscid nonlocal regularisation of the Euler equations. They smooth the flow over a length set by alpha, which tames the wildest small scales. The paper studies the nonlocal-to-local limit: what happens as alpha shrinks to zero.

In the first part, the authors prove convergence of strong solutions. Solutions of the Leray-alpha equations converge to strong solutions of the Euler equations. The result holds in Sobolev spaces for dimensions two and three, for a large class of regularising kernels. Readers get proof that the smoothed model honestly returns the true Euler flow.
arxiv-2601-15613:
Jianxiong Yao and five co-authors build a framework for energy flow in plasmas in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is capacitively coupled plasmas, widely used in industry and research. Electron energy in such plasmas is absorbed, converted, moved, and lost. Grasping each step is essential for reading discharge physics. It also matters for the processes these plasmas run, like etching and coating.

The authors propose a kinetic-moment framework. It rests on particle-in-cell simulations with Monte Carlo collisions. Those simulations track huge numbers of particles and their crashes. Moment methods then summarize the energy story in usable form. Bridging raw simulation and clear physics is the aim. Process engineers rely on such understanding to tune plasma tools.
arxiv-2601-15713:
Jordi José and Margarita Hernanz simulate an exploding star system in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is T Coronae Borealis, a recurrent nova. Recurrent novae erupt more than once. Some are identified by vast super-shells left by past eruptions. Their recurrence times are short, from about one year to a century. That pace sets them apart from ordinary novae.

The authors run hydrodynamic simulations of the system. The goal is to predict nucleosynthesis: which elements the blasts forge. Novae seed space with fresh isotopes. Predicting those yields tests the physics inside the model. T Coronae Borealis draws public interest because its next eruption is awaited. Simulations like these tell observers what chemical signs to look for when it blows.
arxiv-2601-15813:
Clare Chemery, Hendrik Edelhoff, and Ludwig Bothmann build a machine learning pipeline for ecologists in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ecologists increasingly work with image data, from camera traps to field photos. Off-the-shelf models rarely fit local needs. A species mix or habitat can be unique to one study site. The authors offer a lightweight experimentation pipeline instead. It lowers the barrier to applying learning methods on image data.

With it, ecologists can experiment on their own. They can move past generic models and tune to local datasets. Target variables can match the actual research question. The paper targets working scientists, not ML specialists. Tools that hand control to domain experts tend to produce insights that generic pipelines miss. That independence is the point of the design.
arxiv-2601-15913:
Lei Chen, Alice Devillers, Luke Morgan, and Friedrich Rober count colorings that break symmetry in a 2026 arXiv paper. The distinguishing number of a permutation group is defined plainly. It is the fewest colors needed to color the underlying set. The coloring must leave the identity as the only color-preserving group element. Any nontrivial symmetry must disturb some color. The authors compute this number for two graph families.

Complete bipartite graphs and crown graphs are their targets. Both are highly symmetric, so breaking all symmetry with few colors is a puzzle. The fewer the colors, the stronger the result. Distinguishing numbers connect group theory with graph coloring. They also model real tasks, like tagging items so that only the true arrangement looks unchanged.
arxiv-2601-16013:
Ziemowit Kostana, Jarosław Swaczyna, and Agnieszka Widz study infinite random graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Some countable graphs arise from a random process with probability one. Up to isomorphism, the outcome is essentially unique. The Rado graph is the classical example. In that case, each pair of points gets an equal chance of an edge. The authors drop that equal-probability rule. Their graphs allow varied probabilities across pairs.

Unequal chances make the random construction richer. The question is which graphs still arise almost surely. Such universal graphs serve as limits and test cases in logic and combinatorics. A broader construction widens the family of known examples. The paper is in pure mathematics, where clean existence results anchor whole theories.
arxiv-2601-14913:
Nijin J. Thykkathu, Matt J. Jarvis, and the MIGHTEE team ask how the rate of star birth has changed over cosmic time. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses radio waves to trace that history. Radio light is not blocked by dust, unlike much visible light.

Radio views can also be sharp enough to pick out single galaxies. The team works out radio luminosity functions for galaxies that form stars. These functions count how many galaxies shine at each radio brightness. They trace the count out to a redshift near 4.5, deep into the past.
arxiv-2601-15013:
Michael Feil and Julius Lipp speed up a repeated step inside transformer models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with batch inference, where many text sequences run through the model at once. Those sequences often share a common prefix, such as a system prompt.

Standard engines treat each sequence on its own. They recompute the same MLP activations for each copy of the shared prefix. The authors present RadixMLP, which deduplicates that work inside the batch. Shared prefix work is done once, and the savings in time and compute grow with the batch.
arxiv-2601-15413:
Tatiana Pavlidou, Aleks Scholz, and Koraljka Muzic date the young star clusters of the Perseus cloud. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a basic need in astronomy: knowing a cluster's age. Ages let astronomers track how a region formed its stars over time.

The authors test a new way to estimate those ages. It rests on a well-founded assumption: the initial mass function is the same across a star-forming cloud. That means the mix of stellar masses at birth is fixed. From a cluster's mass distribution, its age can then be read off.
arxiv-2601-16313:
Sandra Glotzer, Jeong Rae Kim and Joseph Falson grow NbO films by a heat led growth window. Their 2026 preprint deals with films of niobium oxide, NbO. The team finds a growth mode that turns on past a high heat. Films grown that way beat past films in build and flow. The good mode holds through a range of oxygen push in the growth gas.

Good films form again and again in that range. The team maps the traits that mark the best films. A firm growth window eases work by other labs. It gives a clear recipe for high grade NbO films. Such films serve tests of charge flow in oxides.
arxiv-2601-17113:
J. Sarrato-Alós and a team of five co-authors ask if star birth past shapes dark cores. Dark cores in galaxies can be dense cusps or soft cores. Star birth bursts can stir gas and shift that core. Their 2026 preprint tests that link in fake galaxies. Two famed sim sets, NIHAO and FIRE-2, give the test beds. All galaxies get one same read path.

The team sorts birth past by burst strength and spread. It then sets that sort next to core slope. A firm link would tie bright past to dark shape. Such ties help scopes read real galaxy cores. They test tales of how small galaxies grew.
arxiv-2601-17213:
Asmaa AlMellah, Faeq Abed, and Gaber Faisel study a rare particle process in the scotogenic model. That model links dark matter made of fermions to new scalar particles. The authors look at electron and positron beams that collide. The crash can make a pair of charged scalars, one plus and one minus.

They trace how the pair forms at the lowest order. Paths include exchange of a photon and exchange of a Z boson. A third path swaps new heavy fermions in a side channel. Work like this tells collider teams what signals to hunt for. It also shows how dark matter ideas can be tested in lab crashes.
arxiv-2601-17313:
Briceyda B. Delgado proves a uniqueness result for Calderón's inverse problem. The problem asks what can be learned about the inside of a body from edge measures. It is the math base of electrical impedance tomography. That method sends small currents through a body and reads voltages to map inner conductivity.

Delgado uses integral formulas for solutions of the Vekua equation. The work sits inside Clifford analysis. Links to the conductivity and Schrödinger equations frame the proof. A uniqueness proof says the edge data can pin down one inner state. That ground matters for medical imaging. It tells builders that the map they seek is not a guess among many.
arxiv-2601-17613:
Jingxu Wu, Jie Shi, Chenjia Li, and Yuwei Yin link matter traits to black hole images. They build an explicit linear map for that link. Inputs are compact, conserved changes to the stress-energy tensor. The map gives the metric response in static, spherical spacetimes. From there it yields geometric observables. Key outputs are the shadow radius and photon-sphere frequency.

Those outputs are what horizon-scale imaging measures. A direct map lets teams test matter ideas against photos. It skips long nonlinear solves for small changes. Black hole imaging is now a data-rich field. Fast links from matter to image sharpen its tests. The work serves both gravity theory and observation.
arxiv-2601-18013:
Fei Wan examines whether a matching method lives up to its sales pitch. His 2026 preprint compares coarsened exact matching with propensity score matching. Both methods pair treated and untreated cases to estimate effects fairly. Coarsened exact matching is often sold as the better choice on imbalance, model dependence, bias, and efficiency. Wan argues that the claim is still uncertain, and he gives reasons for doubt.

One reason is a common misreading of the method's name. The matching is not exact on the raw variables; it is exact only after the variables are coarsened into bins. That detail changes what the method can promise. The paper helps applied researchers pick matching tools with open eyes.
arxiv-2601-18213:
Chengkai Huang and co-authors model the whole path of a user's future behavior, not just the next click. Their 2026 preprint presents Generative Chain of Behavior, or GCB. Long-term trajectories matter for understanding how tastes evolve and for timely recommendations. Most sequential recommenders aim only at the next item. That narrow aim misses how one action sets up the next across a long chain. GCB treats user interactions as an autoregressive chain, generating step after step.

A chain view can plan offers and content over weeks, not moments. It can also show where a user's path is likely to fork. The work serves platforms that think in journeys. Predicting the path, not the step, is the shift.
arxiv-2601-19013:
Zeyi Xu and Long Chen build a faster downhill method for convex problems that adapts as it goes. Gradient descent steps against the slope to find a low point, and speed ups exist, but they need true values for smoothness and convexity. Wrong values can slow or break the run.

Their method, A2GD, updates those values as it runs, guided by a Lyapunov style check. Borrowing from the study of steppers for differential equations, it runs a line search only when built up error turns positive. Fewer slope checks, kept guarantees, and no hand tuning make the method handy for large smooth problems.
arxiv-2601-19213:
Weiming Hu and a large team add metadata to tiny number formats so big models lose less accuracy. Low bit microscaling formats store blocks of numbers with one shared power of two scale. That blunt sharing is a main cause of the accuracy drop seen in formats like MXFP4.

Their format, M2XFP, augments the blocks with extra metadata to guide the scaling. Better scales mean each small block hugs its true values more closely. Formats like this decide how cheaply the largest models can be served, since memory and bandwidth rule their cost.
arxiv-2601-19313:
Hetong Wang and three co-authors cancel interference between data streams by shaping waves in the air itself. Stacked intelligent metasurfaces are layers of tunable sheets that bend radio waves as they pass. The team uses them to build a multi stream transmission scheme that aims to be free of interference by design.

Their angle is fresh: instead of fighting interference at the receiver, they exploit it in the wave domain. Constructive interference can add signal rather than noise when the waves are shaped right. Such schemes could lift the capacity of dense wireless links without more spectrum.
arxiv-2601-19413:
Michele Martinelli and a large team design the interconnects that will wire tomorrow's supercomputers and AI clusters. High performance computing blends many cutting edge technologies that must work as one. The wires between nodes, the interconnect, often decide how much of a machine's power real jobs can use.

Their project, NET4EXA, lays out a path for interconnects built for exascale loads and AI traffic. AI training moves vast data between chips, so yesterday's networks strain. A fresh interconnect design is a bet on what the next decade of computing will ask of its plumbing.
arxiv-2601-19513:
Haixu Xi, Heng Zhang, and Chengzhi Zhang address a daily strain on researchers: too many papers to read. Journals and preprint servers now publish at a pace no scholar can follow. A good recommendation system can point each reader to papers that match their needs. That help can raise research efficiency and spark new ideas.

The authors improve recommendations by describing each paper in finer detail. They pull out fine-grained knowledge entities, the specific concepts and terms a paper is built from. They also build document embeddings, numeric summaries of a paper, from several facets at once. Matching readers to papers on these richer signals should beat plain keyword overlap. The work speaks to anyone building search and alert tools for science.
arxiv-2601-19713:
Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, and Mathias B. M. Svendsen study how to move quantum states along a chain of atoms. Rydberg atoms interact over long distances through dipole forces. Those interactions extend two classic models that host topologically protected edge states. Topological protection promises transfer that resists small errors.

The authors build a theoretical framework for state transfer that is fast, robust, and high-fidelity. Speed matters because quantum states decay. Robustness matters because real arrays are imperfect. Long-range couplings complicate the physics but also offer new control. A reliable transfer protocol is a building block for quantum networks and simulators. The work shows how topology can protect information in transit.
arxiv-2601-19913:
Shinwoo Park and Yo-Sub Han ask whether experts can learn to spot machine-written Korean. Even linguistically trained readers struggle to tell human text from fluent model output. They tend to over-trust surface correctness. The authors treat expert detection as a learnable skill that structured training can improve.

They introduce LREAD, a rubric drawn from national Korean writing standards. The rubric targets micro-level artifacts, the tiny tells that separate human from generated text. Readers calibrate their judgement against the rubric. Better detection supports education, publishing, and platform integrity in Korean. The study reframes detection from gut feeling to a trainable craft.
arxiv-2601-20313:
Yiwei Bao, Andrea Addazi, and Shuai Zha build an exact framework for neutrino decoherence in turbulent matter, as found in core-collapse supernovae. Neutrinos streaming through this churning matter lose their quantum coherence, which changes the flavors that detectors later see. The authors use the Nakajima-Zwanzig projection method to derive an exact master equation for the neutrino state.

For turbulence with a red power-law spectrum, the memory term in that equation follows a power law in time. This leads naturally to a fractional calculus description. The framework gives supernova modelers a firmer handle on how flavor signals are reshaped on their way out. The math is hard, but the aim is plain to state.
arxiv-2601-20413:
Nouar Aldahoul and six colleagues study schadenfreude, the pleasure people take in others' misfortune, in Facebook news engagement. Online, this feeling has become a visible, performative part of how news spreads. Yet little is known about how common it is, how it changes, or how it patterns across societies.

The authors analyze ten years of engagement with nine major news publishers. The outlets span the United States, the United Kingdom, and India, with left, right, and centrist papers. A decade-scale map of schadenfreude can show platforms and editors how misfortune-driven engagement shapes public discourse.
arxiv-2601-20613:
The xbench team presents AgentIF-OneDay, a benchmark that tests whether AI agents follow instructions in daily-life tasks. Agent capability on long, complex work keeps growing, with strong results in coding, deep research, and hard problem solving. Yet general users rarely feel those gains in everyday scenarios.

The benchmark works at task level, scoring how well agents carry out ordinary instructions. Daily tasks involve messy context and small steps that lab tests skip. A shared yardstick for them could steer agent design toward usefulness that people notice in normal life, not only in demos.
arxiv-2601-18513:
Kai Hu, Haoqi Hu, and Matt Fredrikson build a new net that can prove its own strength in the face of tricks. Some nets come with a bound that shows no small shift in a shot can flip their call. Past nets with that proof were small, slow to train, or weak on big shot sets. Their net drops two common parts to break that trade.

The net has no folds of the classic kind and no hard caps that slow its growth. It trains by steps that keep its weights on a curved space where the bound holds by form. A new part shifts the shot to catch form with no folds at all. The team bill it as the first net of its kind to reach huge scale. Such nets could serve fields where a proof of strength is a must, not a plus.
arxiv-2601-18913:
Mohammad Elayan and Wissam Kontar learn the trade-offs of self-drive cars straight from real road data. A self-drive car must weigh three aims at once. It must stay safe, it must not waste time, and it must deal well with the cars and folk near it. A gain in one aim can cost in the next. Past work set those weights by hand or by a plan, not by how cars truly drive.

The team score each tick of real drives on all three aims. Those scores chart the space of trades that real drives make. A car can then be set to a point in that space by choice, with eyes open. The chart is built in parts, so each aim's score can be checked on its own. Such a chart could help firms set drive style with care.
arxiv-2601-18813:
Matthias Gehnen and Julius Stannat study a chess form in which each side sees just part of the board. In that form, called Fog of War chess, a player knows where their own men stand but not where the foe's men hide. A move can land on a hid foe and take it, or walk in-to a trap. The form is played a lot on-line, but its maths was bare.

The pair give the first strict study of its end phase, when few men are left. With few men, the fog thins and the game turns on what each side can work out of past takes and checks. Their work maps which end states are wins, which are draws, and how the fog shifts the worth of each man. A strict base could guide both play and the bots that learn the form.
arxiv-2601-21213:
Gaofeng Wang, Weike Wang, and Tianfang Wu study the Boltzmann equation for gas mixtures whose molecules have different masses. The equation tracks how the spread of molecule speeds changes over time and space. Most past work treats a single kind of gas.

Mixtures with unequal masses behave in richer ways, since light and heavy molecules trade energy at different rates. The authors prove that classic smooth solutions exist for this harder case. Their result fills a gap in the theory of gases. It also supports models of real mixtures, from air to industrial gas flows, where mass gaps are the norm.
arxiv-2601-21613:
Hugo Morvan, Jonas Agholme, and co-authors present a software package for filling gaps in very large datasets. Missing data are common in big medical registries, where they can bias results if handled badly. Multiple imputation fills each gap several times to reflect the doubt around it.

Their package, bigMICE, scales that process to data too large for standard tools. It was built with Swedish health quality registries in mind. Registries guide real care decisions, so honest handling of missing values matters. The tool lets analysts keep the rigor of imputation without shrinking their data to fit old software.
arxiv-2601-22313:
Yavuz Bakman, Duygu Nur Yaldiz, Salman Avestimehr, and Sai Praneeth Karimireddy warn that a clean test today may not keep a model safe tomorrow. Their 2026 preprint notes that large models are updated often in real use. Past work shows updates can strip safety traits or revive facts meant to be erased.

They call the risk hair-trigger alignment: a small update flips the model back. Checks done from outside, with no view of the weights, cannot rule it out. The claim presses teams to test after each update, not just at launch. It reshapes how release gates should work.
arxiv-2601-22413:
Carlos Segovia links the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famed open claim in math, to a grid of number partitions. The hypothesis concerns where a key function hits zero, and it governs how primes spread. His 2026 preprint uses a known equivalent form of the claim.

That form rests on a threshold for how large a divisor-sum can grow. Segovia builds a direct bridge from that form to the Young lattice, a grid that sorts box diagrams. A new bridge gives attackers of the claim a fresh path. It may also reveal why the threshold takes its odd value. The work is a link, not a proof.
arxiv-2601-22713:
D. Vincenzi reports a beam test of a hybrid photon detector that reads single photons with fine timing. The device pairs a microchannel plate tube with a CMOS chip sealed inside. His 2026 preprint describes its run in a high-energy hadron beam at CERN, in a Cherenkov setup.

The detector ran at high gain and timed photons to a few hundred picoseconds. Fast, sure photon timing serves particle physics and imaging alike. A sealed, chip-read design could scale to large detectors. The test shows the concept works in a real beam. That proof is the paper's core.
arxiv-2601-20813:
Anna Fino, Gueo Grantcharov, and Jose Medel construct new solutions to a system from geometry and physics. Their 2026 paper concerns the Hull-Strominger system with G2 symmetry. They build the solutions as torus fibrations over K3 orbifolds. A fibration stacks copies of a torus over each point of a base space. Here the base is a singular K3 surface.

The construction starts with three chosen divisors on that surface. They must be primitive with respect to a particular Kähler metric. The stable bundle then comes from an adapted Serre construction, moved into the singular setting. The total spaces are principal torus bundles over the K3 surfaces. The result adds fresh examples to a system that links complex geometry with string theory. Such examples help test what the theory can produce.
arxiv-2601-21013:
Chinmay Kulkarni and a large team of co-authors assemble a twenty-seven-year record of young stars flickering. Their 2026 paper surveys large-amplitude variability in young stellar objects. Infrared light can probe this variability across the full range of youth. The span runs from deeply embedded protostars to pre-main-sequence stars with dusty disks. The team built light curves from 1997 to 2024.

Three space telescopes supply the record. They are ISO, Spitzer, and WISE with its NEOWISE phase. All observed in the infrared, between three and eight microns. Stitching their archives gives one long, uniform view. Big brightness swings can signal bursts of accretion or clearing dust. The survey lets astronomers count how common such drama is. It is a legacy dataset for the study of how stars grow.
arxiv-2512-01213:
Yangbangyan Jiang and co-authors work on a score used to judge sorting models. The full score counts how well a model ranks good cases above bad ones. A partial score looks at just one slice of that rank. That slice matters when false alarms must stay very low.

Two ways to train for the partial score had a gap between them. The team works to close that gap. Closing it means the score seen in training matches the score that counts in use. Gains here help fields like disease tests and fraud checks, where low false alarm rates are key.
arxiv-2512-00813:
Savitha K S, Sandi Klavžar, and Tijo James study a two-player graph game in a 2025 paper. In the Maker-Breaker resolving game, two players take turns claiming unplayed vertices of a graph. One player, Resolver, wants to claim every vertex of some resolving set. A resolving set pins down all vertices by their distances to it.

The other player, Spoiler, wants to grab at least one vertex from every resolving set, blocking Resolver. The authors study the game on lexicographic products, a way of building big graphs from smaller ones. Knowing who wins helps judge how robust location schemes on networks can be.
arxiv-2512-01113:
Dongyue Li and four coauthors teach branching networks for multitask reasoning in a 2025 paper. Algorithmic reasoning, following step-by-step logical procedures, is a core benchmark for graph neural networks and large language models. Ideally one model would handle many algorithmic tasks at once, rather than a separate model per task.

Learning many procedures together is hard, since tasks interfere and need different steps at different times. Their branching networks learn to route computation so one model can perform well across tasks. Efficient multitask reasoning would cut the cost of serving many narrow models, and test whether machines can share skills across procedures.
arxiv-2601-23013:
Ernesto Benitez-Walz and four co-authors characterize faint stellar streams with self-supervised learning. Stellar streams are ribbons of stars torn from galaxies and clusters, glowing very dimly. Studying them reveals how the Milky Way grew by swallowing smaller systems.

They apply a nearest-neighbor contrastive method to a curated part of the Dark Energy Survey's second data release. The method learns from the images themselves, without hand labels. Automated stream-finding could survey far more sky than manual inspection allows. Low surface brightness features are the target, the faint tidal debris that wide-field surveys record but rarely catalog well.
arxiv-2601-23213:
Roberto Rubboli, Erkka Haapasalo, and Marco Tomamichel characterize all valid forms of conditional entropy. Entropies measure uncertainty, with central roles in information theory, statistics, and the quantitative sciences. Under natural operational axioms, the most general entropy is the Rényi family, indexed by one real parameter.

Conditional entropy, uncertainty given side information, needed its own full characterization. The authors supply it, showing exactly which functions can serve. A complete axiomatic map prevents ad hoc measures and anchors quantum and classical information theory alike. The Rényi family, parameterized by a single real number, frames the conditional characterization the authors complete.
arxiv-2512-00113:
Neuromorphic processors copy some design ideas from the brain to run AI with very little power. Amirreza Yousefzadeh offers a tutorial on building scalable digital versions of them in 2025. The tutorial starts from RISC-V cores and moves toward arrays of neuromorphic units.

Digital neuromorphic chips suit low-power, always-on edge applications, such as sensors that must react without waking a larger system. The author lays out the main architectural design principles and illustrates them with the SENECA platform as a running example. New engineers entering the field get a guided path through the design choices involved. Tutorials like this one lower the entry barrier for a fast-moving hardware field.
arxiv-2512-00213:
Random connection models scatter points in space and link nearby pairs, forming clusters that can suddenly span the whole system. Mikhail Chebunin and Günter Last study the sharp phase transition in such a model in 2025. The points come from a Poisson process with a given intensity.

The authors derive exponential moment bounds for an arbitrary cluster when the intensity stays below a critical value. Strong bounds of this kind prove the transition is genuinely sharp, not gradual. These models describe wireless networks and material structures, so knowing exactly where giant clusters appear has practical as well as theoretical value. Exponential bounds are strong evidence, ruling out slowly growing giant clusters below threshold.
arxiv-2512-00613:
The Hubbard model is the simplest model that still captures how electron interactions create magnets and insulators. Fahad Equbal and Ahsan study the Mott crossover in the half-filled Hubbard model in 2025, resolved by spin. They use exact diagonalization on a small square cluster.

The crossover runs from a correlated metallic state to a Mott-insulating state as interaction strength grows. The authors examine both spin sectors and the entanglement between electrons. Even small clusters, solved exactly, benchmark the approximations used for real materials where no exact solution exists. Exact diagonalization is exact but tiny, which is why the small square cluster matters as a benchmark. Entanglement tracks how inseparable the electrons' states become across the crossover.
arxiv-2512-03113:
Water flow through soil and rock is hard to predict fast. Zhenglong Chen and five co-authors offer a learning-based shortcut in this 2025 work. The flow, called Darcy flow, changes over time and depends on random traits of the porous material.

Their method blends time coding, operator learning, and a U-shaped network. It learns to map random inputs to flow fields across space and time. A fast stand-in model can replace slow simulations in design and planning. That speed helps in groundwater, oil, and carbon storage studies. For flow modelers, adaptive sampling focuses effort where the field changes fastest.
arxiv-2512-03213:
Fake projective planes look like a classic surface but are not. Lev Borisov and Bojue Wang find explicit equations for a new pair in this 2025 work. The pair is labeled in the Cartwright-Steger classification of these rare surfaces.

Explicit equations let other mathematicians compute with the surfaces directly. Fake projective planes are scarce and hard to construct, so each new pair matters. Their equations can test ideas in complex geometry and number theory. The work adds concrete examples to a field that has few of them. Each new fake plane tests the classification scheme that predicts which types can exist.
arxiv-2512-03313:
A famous counterexample in dynamics leaves an open question. Yi Liu and Lin Wang revisit Herman's converse KAM mechanism in this 2025 work. Herman built a perturbation of an integrable system from two parts: a hyperbolic term and a bump function.

Herman himself noted it was unclear whether the bump function was truly needed. Liu and Wang return to that remark and examine the mechanism again. KAM theory concerns which motions survive small disturbances. Settling Herman's question sharpens the border between stable and chaotic dynamics. Bump functions look minor, yet they can decide whether a counterexample truly works.
arxiv-2512-02013:
Robots guided by vision-language-action models can understand scenes and act, yet long jobs with a defined end state, like assembling LEGO or rearranging objects, still defeat them. Chenyang Gu and co-authors present ManualVLA in 2025, a single model that both writes a step-by-step manual and carries it out.

The model uses chain-of-thought reasoning to generate the manual, then follows it during manipulation, joining high-level planning with precise hand control. Splitting the two abilities across separate systems is what earlier approaches did, and the seams showed on long tasks. A unified model that plans in words and then acts offers a cleaner path to dependable robot helpers.
arxiv-2512-02213:
Chatbots serve low-resource languages poorly, largely because good instruction datasets for training them are scarce and hard to build. Mamadou Keita and three co-authors present InstructLR in 2025, a scalable approach to creating such datasets, aimed at languages spoken across Africa and other underserved regions.

Effective text generation needs many examples of instructions paired with good responses, in the language itself. Curating those by hand for hundreds of languages does not scale, so a systematic generation approach is required. Better instruction data is the most direct route to language technology that works for the majority of the world's speakers.
arxiv-2512-02413:
Turning a flat floor plan into a 3D model starts with finding the walls, thin lines that segmentation models easily miss or blur. Dmitriy Parashchuk, Alexey Kapshitskiy, and Yuriy Karyakin introduce MitUNet in 2025, a hybrid network for precise wall segmentation in floor plan recognition.

The design pairs a Mix-Transformer encoder with a U-Net decoder, reinforced by spatial and channel attention blocks. That combination targets both thin structures and geometric precision, the two known weak points. Accurate automatic reconstruction of indoor spaces feeds renovation planning, real estate tools, and robot navigation maps.
arxiv-2512-02513:
Krishnendu S. Tharakan and Carlo Fischione tackle the hard task of streaming virtual reality over wireless links. Wireless VR frees users to move anywhere, but the video must stay sharp, smooth, and nearly instant. Headsets also have limited computing power, which tightens every design choice.

Their 2025 study uses federated learning, where devices train a shared model without sending raw data away. The design is decentralized and fairness aware, so weaker devices are not left behind. Multi task training lets one model serve several VR needs at once, saving bandwidth and battery. Fair shares keep small headsets in the loop, not locked out by weak links or low charge.
arxiv-2512-02713:
Theodoros Aivalis and three co-authors trace which training images shaped what an image generator produces. As generative models grow stronger, questions of credit, transparency, and copyright grow sharper. Knowing which data drove an output is central to answering them fairly.

Their framework builds ontology aligned knowledge graphs automatically to interpret generated outputs. Concepts in the graph link an image back to the data and ideas behind it. Such traceability could help artists seek credit, help auditors check datasets, and help builders explain their models to regulators and users. Graphs of this kind can be read by staff who know no code, which broadens who can audit a tool.
arxiv-2512-02913:
Underwater optical links promise fast data through the sea, but turbulence in the water fights the beam. A Gaussian light beam crossing a turbulent underwater channel suffers fading and scattering. Even weak turbulence can severely degrade communication quality, the study notes.

The analysis covers multi wavelength channels, comparing how several colors of light perform at once. Knowing which wavelengths hold up best guides design of links for divers, submarines, and ocean sensors. Reliable underwater optics would ease inspection, science, and rescue work where radio fails quickly. More than one hue at once gives a link a spare path when one hue fades, a cheap form of back up for sea gear.
plos-pone-0010013:
Christian Stegmann, Reinhard Lührmann, and Markus Wahl reported a protein structure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was PPIL1, a small enzyme that sits inside the spliceosome, the machine that cuts introns out of RNA messages. PPIL1 also binds a partner protein called SKIP through a site apart from its active center.

The team solved the crystal structure of PPIL1 bound to the drug cyclosporine A. From that shape, they proposed how a straight stretch of SKIP might bind. Knowing the shape helps explain how the splicing machine holds together and how drugs can grip one of its parts.
plos-pone-0010213:
The authors were Laura Heath, Susan Conway, Laura Jones, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined HIV passing from mother to child in breast milk. Breast milk transmission remains a major route of infection in children. When a baby is infected, usually only one or few viral variants succeed, a narrow event called a genetic bottleneck.

The team asked whether milk itself holds only restricted viral types, explaining that bottleneck. Their answer was no: restriction in milk does not account for it. The filter must act later, during or after the virus crosses into the child.
plos-pone-0009813:
Brain-computer interfaces let people control devices with brain signals alone. Martijn Schreuder, Benjamin Blankertz, and Michael Tangermann presented a new auditory version in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most earlier systems relied on vision instead of hearing.

The paradigm uses spatial hearing, the sense of where a sound comes from, as its cue. Different sound positions stand for different choices the user can select. A multi-class system offers more than two options at once. It also widens the options for hands-free control. Hearing-based control could help users who cannot rely on their eyes.
plos-pone-0009913:
Anthrax lethal toxin can kill immune cells, yet some cells learn to tolerate it. Nando Dulal Das and colleagues studied that tolerance in a mouse immune cell line. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tolerance here means surviving doses that should kill.

The cells were RAW 264.7, a standard macrophage line. Two players stood out: NF-kappa-B, a master immune switch, and Jmjd3, an enzyme that removes a histone mark called H3K27me3. Removing that mark can free silenced genes to speak. The pairing may explain how the cells endure the toxin.
